headline: The falling hazard in agent time-horizon curves is between-task frailty, not within-task degradation: hold the task fixed and the per-minute hazard is flat.
current_belief: Hamilton (Jan 2026) fits a pooled Weibull with shape about 0.6 for frontier agents and reads it as the agents' hazard; Ord 2505.05115 reads a half-life; METR's own logistic-in-log-time curve is the sigma^2 = 1 gamma-frailty curve without being named as one (X-2026-W42-S7F9, derivation in the seed record)
if_true: Horizon producers publish the frailty variance or the within-task run agreement beside every 50% and 80% horizon and label the 80% horizon a share of tasks within reach; forecasters use k_cond for single-task tails and sigma^2 for reach; pass^k reporters replace one per-step reliability with a per-task distribution
if_false: The within-task hazard falls too (k_cond well below 1): agents do degrade along a task, which makes the horizon curve a property of agents after all and makes the step-clock hazard shape (S7xF9) the next question
probes: X-2026-W42-S7F9 (frailty refit of METR-Horizon-v1.1 runs; $0, 3 d; no scorecard)
import:2026-W43-S7xF9 (step-clock hazard on tau-bench; ~$300-600 + 60 GPU-h; no scorecard)

headline: The run-to-run variance that agent benchmarks report at temperature 0 is the serving stack's batch-dependent arithmetic, not the agent, and over multi-turn trajectories it is large enough to reorder leaderboards.
raised_by: Jacob, 2026-10-20 03:13 ET, in chat: Thinking Machines' post on defeating nondeterminism in LLM inference is adjacent to our luck-subtraction thread
current_belief: Fetched 2026-10-20 from thinkingmachines.ai/blog/defeating-nondeterminism-in-llm-inference (Horace He and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025-09-10): the forward pass is run-to-run deterministic, but kernels whose reduction order changes with batch size make a request's numerics depend on the other requests in the batch, so 'from each user's perspective the output is nondeterministic'; Qwen3-235B-A22B at temperature 0, 1000 completions of 1000 tokens: 80 unique completions, identical for the first 102 tokens; with batch-invariant kernels all 1000 identical; cost on Qwen3-8B, 1000 sequences: 26 s default vs 55 s unoptimised vs 42 s with the improved attention kernel (about 2.1x and 1.6x). The post frames this as reproducibility and on-policy RL (sampler-trainer KL flat at 0) and does not discuss benchmark evaluation. The field's working belief to test at the kill search: temperature-0 agent evaluations are reported as single runs or with a 'noise' of a point or two, as if deterministic.
if_true: Every temperature-0 benchmark report states its serving stack and whether decoding was batch-invariant; leaderboards add a stack-noise column or run batch-invariant; and the per-turn luck-skill decomposition (W41 product red team C, parked) becomes exactly identifiable on the agent side: a batch-invariant agent at temperature 0 has zero decision variance by construction, so Var[R] decomposes onto the user simulator and environment alone - the control arm that instrument lacked.
if_false: At trajectory scale the token-level divergences rarely change an action's outcome (flip rate under 2 percent, rank order stable) - a reassuring measurement benchmark owners would still cite when they report temperature-0 numbers; the luck-skill thread stays parked on its consumer verdict.
relates_to: W41 product red team C: per-turn luck/skill attribution for user-simulator benchmarks (parked in L1; data/reports/2026-W41-product-redteam-C.md) - this claim supplies the exact zero-variance agent arm that the split needed
standards.md Gate 0: 'a party at temperature 0 has zero decision variance by construction' now holds only with batch-invariant decoding; without it, temperature 0 is a protocol artifact
probes: P-W43-J01-a (thought; 15-25 GPU-h, $50-80, 4 days): outcome-flip rate at temperature 0, default stack vs batch-invariant, on a multi-turn agent benchmark with open models

P-W43-J01-a.what: Outcome-flip rate at temperature 0: default serving stack (batch composition varied by concurrency) versus batch-invariant decoding, agent and user simulator both an 8B open model at temperature 0, on a multi-turn benchmark with deterministic tools
P-W43-J01-a.design: Two arms x 10 repeats x 100 tasks. Default arm: vLLM default kernels, each repeat run at a different concurrency (alone, 8, 32) so batch composition changes. Treatment arm: the same stack with batch-invariant kernels (TML's released kernels or vLLM's batch-invariant mode - which exists and works for the model is checked at the kill search); its flip rate must be exactly 0, which is the determinism check. Record per task: any outcome disagreement across the 10 repeats, the turn of first divergence, pass^k for k=1..10, and the rank order of three agent variants (prompt or scaffold variants) per repeat.
P-W43-J01-a.kill_probe: Dead if the default arm's outcome-flip rate is under 2 percent of tasks AND the rank order of the three agent variants is identical across all ten repeats. Expected (judgment): 5-15 percent flips on 30-turn tasks and at least one adjacent-rank swap. Field's assumption: temperature 0 is deterministic or noise of a point. Belief-changing: over 15 percent or a non-adjacent rank reversal. 15-25 GPU-hours on one H100, $50-80, 4 days.
neighbors_to_check_first: the TML post and the kernels it released (2025-09-10)
vLLM and SGLang deterministic or batch-invariant inference modes (dates and coverage)
any paper measuring temperature-0 output nondeterminism of LLMs or agents across runs (search: nondeterminism, 'temperature 0', reproducibility, batch, variance, agent benchmark)
benchmark reports that run agents at temperature 0 and how they report variance (tau-bench, SWE-bench, terminal-bench - read their own text)

scorecard.target_value: Asked in print: the TML post (fetched) calls reproducibility 'a bedrock of scientific progress' and shows 80 unique completions in 1000 at temperature 0, but stops before evaluation - that is the gap. Who pays: benchmark owners who report temperature-0 numbers, and anyone ranking agents a few points apart. Missing: a benchmark owner's own statement about temperature-0 variance - kill search.

impact_ceiling.floor: A measured flip-rate and first-divergence-turn table for one benchmark and one model; a note people cite when they report temperature-0 numbers. Requires the probe. p = 0.7 (judgment).
impact_ceiling.middle: The number is large enough that benchmark owners add a serving-stack column or adopt batch-invariant decoding for official runs. Requires flips over 5 percent or a rank swap. p = 0.25 (judgment).
impact_ceiling.ceiling: The exact zero-variance agent arm re-opens the parked per-turn luck-skill instrument with a clean identification, and the pair becomes a standards paper on deterministic evaluation of agents. Requires the middle result plus the parked item's consumer objection answered. p = 0.1 (judgment).

scorecard.relevance: L1 (reliability, variance attribution): direct. L3 and the systems route (Lloyd, Netravali, Dao): batch-invariant kernels are their vocabulary; direct. Narasimhan route via tau-bench as the natural testbed. Industry: every eval team. Jacob's edge: GPU numerics and kernels (computer engineering) load-bearing. Zero for L5 and for any robotics consumer.
scorecard.kill_probe: P-W43-J01-a above: 15-25 GPU-h, $50-80, 4 days; dead if flips under 2 percent and ranks identical across ten repeats.
scorecard.density_and_ownership: Unknown until the kill search (12-month arXiv API count with mechanism words - batch invariance, reduction order, nondeterminism - AND role words - benchmark, evaluation, agent, pass^k; two pre-window precedents; the two closest papers' limitation text). Incumbents to check: TML's kernels, vLLM/SGLang deterministic modes, any 'temperature 0 is not deterministic' measurement.
scorecard.why_now: Batch-invariant kernels (2025-09-10) make a truly zero-variance agent arm available for the first time; before them, stack noise and agent decision variance at temperature 0 could not be separated, so nobody could measure the first in isolation.
scorecard.register: Measurement (a ruler for serving-stack noise at benchmark scale) with a standards consequence (what a temperature-0 report must state). It is not a new kernel, not a benchmark, not a method, and not a claim about sampling at temperature above 0.

decisions: Is this worth its kill search slot this week (it would take one of the three), given it serves L1 and the systems route rather than the top-ranked L5 thread?
history: captured from chat (Jacob raised the TML nondeterminism post as adjacent to the luck-subtraction thread); scorecard skeleton filled where the fetched post supports it; kill search owed before it is a proposal

P-W43-01-2x2.status: thought (spec written in the 2026-10-21 discuss session; scorecard and kill search owed before it is a candidate)
P-W43-01-2x2.what: The simulator-budget 2x2: train a policy at the shipped solver budget (Go1 iterations=1; Leap iterations=5) and at the converged budget (iterations=100, tol 1e-8) under the full training protocol (DR, kicks, observation noise, sampled actions) with a wall-clock-matched arm; evaluate every policy in both engines with paired DR draws and seeds; the interaction term J_conv(pi_conv) - J_conv(pi_cap) - [J_cap(pi_conv) - J_cap(pi_cap)] is the cap-isolated exploit; the certificate ||g_K|| and nchange logged per step are the fidelity column; sim2sim across engines (Playground's shipped script) is the field-standard transfer proxy; hardware is the ceiling arm.
P-W43-01-2x2.kill_probe: Dead if the interaction term lies inside the batch-seed interval of zero on BOTH Go1 rough terrain and the Leap cube task. Pre-registered (judgment): Go1 interaction about zero (sticking contacts; the hardware prior), Leap interaction positive and a non-trivial share of return (many simultaneous contacts; SAPU's interpenetration exploit in assembly is the precedent). Field's assumption: DR absorbs numerical error everywhere, and Leap failures are hardware flex and geometry. Belief-changing: a positive Leap interaction that shrinks with budget at matched wall-clock. Cost: two retrains per task at minutes each on 2 GPUs, cross-evaluation in minutes; 4-10 GPU-hours including the Leap retrain (no public Leap checkpoint), $20-50, one week.

source: chat
headline: A GPU simulator's physics budget is a dose: transferable policy return follows one dose-response curve in solver budget per task class, so fidelity can be scheduled during training like a learning rate instead of fixed by a config file.
raised_by: Jacob and the operator, 2026-10-21 discuss session on the simulator thread (the systems half of L5, now framed as the consequence of a measurement)
current_belief: Solver budgets are fixed per task in model files (Playground XML iterations=1 Go1, 5 Leap; legged_gym num_position_iterations=4) and justified by DR (MJX docs, fetched 2026-10-20 in the C-W43-15 red team); numerical settings are treated as a randomization axis (Dactyl randomized the time step), not a dial; the only fetched RL consumer of a fidelity scalar is a control-variate estimator (MFPG-PPO 2610.02505).
if_true: Training recipes gain a fidelity schedule (coarse early, converged late) at matched wall-clock; engine teams expose the budget per world as a runtime knob rather than a file constant; the iteration-level scheduler (the lane's systems piece) has a stated consumer.
if_false: Response is task-specific or non-monotone: fixed budgets are right and the scheduler has no consumer - a result engine teams would still cite when choosing defaults.
probes: P-W43-01-2x2 (rides on CL-W43-01's probe: the dose-response of transferable return in budget comes free from the 2x2 plus two intermediate budgets)
C-W43-16 (compute-matched fidelity mixture vs fixed cap in GPU RL; 50 GPU-h, $150, 7 d) - the recipe test

P-W43-01-2x2.what: Dose-response arm of the 2x2: add budgets {2, 10} to {shipped, 100}; plot transferable return (evaluated in the converged engine and in a second engine) against budget at matched wall-clock.
P-W43-01-2x2.kill_probe: Dead for this claim if the curves for Go1 and Leap are not monotone or do not share a shape up to scale (pre-registered: Spearman of the two normalised curves above 0.8); then budgets are task constants, not a dose. Cost rides on CL-W43-01's probe (+2 budgets, +2-4 GPU-h).

scorecard.target_value: Asked in print: 2610.17221's recipe needs a known fidelity law and declines the solver axis (fetched 2026-10-19); MFPG-PPO uses a low-fidelity simulator as a control variate without isolating any knob. Who pays: anyone training in GPU simulators under a wall-clock budget; engine teams choosing defaults.

impact_ceiling.floor: Two dose-response curves on public tasks; a note cited when budgets are chosen. p = 0.6 (judgment).
impact_ceiling.middle: A shared curve shape licenses a fidelity schedule; C-W43-16 shows it beats fixed budgets at matched wall-clock; Playground or Isaac Lab exposes the knob. p = 0.2 (judgment).
impact_ceiling.ceiling: Fidelity scheduling becomes a standard training lever and the iteration-level scheduler ships inside an engine. p = 0.05 (judgment) - this scenario is head-to-head with engine teams and is reached only from a lab position.

scorecard.relevance: L5 direct; the systems route (GPU scheduling) via the scheduler consequence; robotics faculty via training recipes; Jacob's edge (numerics, GPU scheduling) load-bearing; zero for L1-L2 and LLM consumers.
scorecard.kill_probe: Rides on the 2x2 (+2-4 GPU-h): dead if curves are non-monotone or do not share a shape.
scorecard.density_and_ownership: Unknown until the kill search; incumbents: engine defaults, MFPG-PPO (bundled knobs), curriculum-over-fidelity work in other fields (to search: multi-fidelity optimisation, progressive refinement - PRDP 2502.19611 is the linear-solver precedent).
scorecard.why_now: Minutes-scale training in GPU engines (Playground, Feb 2025) makes a budget sweep a one-day job; before, each point was a day.
scorecard.register: Measurement (a dose-response) with a recipe consequence (a schedule) and, only from a lab position, a systems artifact. Not a new engine, not a contact model.

headline: The fidelity scores physics engines report do not predict whether policies trained in them transfer; the worst-case physical violation a budgeted optimiser can extract from the engine does.
raised_by: Jacob and the operator, 2026-10-23: the consequence claim of the simulator meta-benchmark (data/threads/PROGRAM-L5-simulators.md, Part II)
current_belief: Engines and simulator benchmarks report average fidelity on chosen motions: GPUSimBench 2607.13059 (fetched) scores distributional alignment of an inclined-plane task with real data; RGBench 2511.06434 (fetched) scores simulated garment dynamics against measured real ones and reports a 20 percent error reduction; 2603.14634 (fetched) ships analytical-solution tests for rigid bodies. Policy-Aware Simulator Learning 2605.29032 (fetched) argues the right objective for LEARNED simulators is strategic robustness to an adversarial policy rather than predictive accuracy, and proves the worst-case policy is dual to RL on the critic's one-step error - the same move for engineered simulators is unmeasured. Whether any reported fidelity number predicts sim-to-real transfer is, in the fetched set, untested (density check at the kill search; arXiv API throttled on 2026-10-23).
if_true: Engine releases and simulator benchmarks report an exploitability curve beside fidelity; robot-RL authors quote it when they claim transfer; synthetic-data and world-model builders audit their generators with it; the ruler becomes a reviewer's ask.
if_false: Either both predict (then the cheap fidelity number suffices and the adaptive layer is a service) or neither does (then transfer is governed by modelling error outside the engine's numerics, a result that redirects the lane to validation against real data).
probes: P-W43-J03-a (thought; $0 + 20-60 GPU-h, 3 weeks): on the public paired sim/real policy tables already in our records (R2S-Eval, SimFoundry, Kaedim 2610.00731, SIMPLER), compute the ruler's fidelity functionals and an exploitability curve in each simulator used, and correlate both with the measured real-sim disagreement

P-W43-J03-a.what: Predictivity test on existing paired data: for every (policy, simulator) pair in the public real-to-sim tables used in CL-W43-02 (tens of triples), compute (i) the mean fidelity functionals along the policy's own rollouts (energy-from-nothing, complementarity residual, metamorphic defects, Richardson error) and (ii) the exploitability curve X(B) of that simulator on that task under a fixed optimiser budget; correlate each with the real-sim outcome gap (rank agreement with chance correction).
P-W43-J03-a.kill_probe: Pre-registered: dead if neither family reaches Spearman 0.3 with the gap (ruler is a service), and dead as a headline if fidelity predicts as well as exploitability (adaptive layer adds nothing). Expected (judgment): fidelity under 0.2, exploitability above 0.5 on contact-rich tasks. Power is limited by tens of triples; report intervals. Cost: fidelity side $0 (public policies and simulators); exploitability side 20-60 GPU-h ($60-200); 3 weeks.

headline: At the settings they ship, physics engines differ in what a budgeted optimiser can extract from them by more than their fidelity scores differ, and their speed claims reorder once speed is quoted at a fixed accuracy.
raised_by: Jacob, non-rigid session 2026-10-23 ('grade engines by their worst exploitable error, and quote speed only at a fixed accuracy'), captured by the operator with the ruler of PROGRAM-L5-simulators.md Part II under it
current_belief: Engine speed is reported at the engine's own settings and fidelity on chosen motions (GPUSimBench 2607.13059, fetched: scalability and distributional fidelity at fixed settings, soft bodies excluded; RGBench 2511.06434, fetched: 20 percent lower error at 3x the speed on garments). Exploitation of simulators is folklore with a standard answer, domain randomization (Peng 2017, fetched in the C-W43-15 red team), and no engine reports an exploitability number. IcFuzz 2608.06088 (fetched) fuzzes Isaac Sim for crashes, not for physics violations.
if_true: Engine comparisons quote exploits per GPU-hour and time-to-accuracy; the speed leaderboard reorders; synthetic-data generators choose engines by exploitability for their task class.
if_false: All engines break at once or none does (the ruler cannot separate engines - its functionals are the problem), or exploitability ranks engines exactly as fidelity does (nothing new) - either is a usable finding about the ruler, not about the engines.
probes: P-W43-J04-a (thought; 10-30 GPU-h, $30-100, 2 weeks): exploitability curves X(B) for three engines on one cloth task and one rigid-contact task, adversary = gradients where the engine is differentiable, CEM or PPO otherwise, reward = the dimensionless violation functionals; speed re-measured at fixed Richardson error

P-W43-J04-a.what: Two tasks (a cloth task with public real data - the 2024 cloth sim-to-real benchmark or RGBench garments - and the Leap or Go1 rigid-contact task), three engines each (candidates: MuJoCo/MJX, Genesis, Isaac Lab deformables, SOFA, DaXBench for a differentiable cloth arm). For each engine-task, run an optimiser with budget B in {0.5, 2, 5} GPU-h whose reward is the energy-from-nothing plus complementarity plus metamorphic violation, dimensionless; record X(B). Re-measure wall-clock at a fixed Richardson error target instead of at shipped settings.
P-W43-J04-a.kill_probe: Pre-registered: dead if every engine's X(5 GPU-h) exceeds a gross violation (all break instantly) or none exceeds the batch-permutation floor (none breaks) - no separation; dead as a headline if the X ranking equals the fidelity ranking and the speed ranking is unchanged at fixed accuracy. Expected (judgment): separation of 3-10x in X at B = 2 GPU-h between the fastest and the most conservative engine on cloth; at least one speed-rank swap at fixed accuracy. 10-30 GPU-h, $30-100, 2 weeks.
neighbors_to_check_first: GPUSimBench 2607.13059 (speed, determinism, inclined-plane fidelity; what it excludes)
the 2024 cloth sim-to-real benchmark (four engines scored against real cloth recordings)
2304.06372 (NCP violation as the solver criterion)
Stone Tao's Genesis speed critique (blog; benchmark scope)
Erez, Tassa, Todorov ICRA 2015 (the CPU-era speed-vs-accuracy comparison)

Who pays: anyone budgeting synthetic data or choosing an engine for a task class.

impact_ceiling.middle: Engine comparisons adopt exploits-per-GPU-hour and time-to-accuracy; one engine changes a default or ships a regression test on the ruler. p = 0.2 (judgment).
impact_ceiling.ceiling: The ruler is the per-release card for engines (with claim A behind it). p = 0.1 (judgment).

neighbors.difference: Trace-free predictor at the policy level; the competing predictor claim A races against.

neighbors.title: Sim2Real Predictivity (Kadian et al. 2019)
neighbors.trick: Run nine navigation models in a scanned lab and its replica; SRCC 0.18 because agents exploited collision dynamics by sliding along walls; 0.844 after tuning the simulator.
neighbors.difference: The single-artifact datum behind claim A; post-hoc, one engine, no exploitability measurement.

neighbors.title: Imperfect World Models are Exploitable
neighbors.trick: A model is exploitable when it ranks two policies oppositely to the true dynamics; exploitation is unavoidable on large policy sets.
neighbors.difference: Theory of the object our 2x2 interaction measures; no measurement, no engines.

neighbors.title: Policy-Aware Simulator Learning
neighbors.trick: Train a learned simulator as a minimax game against an adversarial policy whose worst case is dual to RL on the critic's one-step error.
neighbors.difference: Needs the true environment to score error; ours scores conservation-law violations with no oracle on engineered engines.

neighbors.title: Predicting Sim-to-Real Transfer with Probabilistic Dynamics Models
neighbors.trick: Score a dynamics model trained with the policy on a fixed set of real trajectories; the score predicts transfer of training setups.
neighbors.difference: Needs real trajectories; no simulator property.

neighbors.title: PolySim
neighbors.trick: Train across several engines so a policy cannot overfit one; the exploit is measured as a sim-to-sim success drop.
neighbors.difference: Whole-engine exploit test, the field's standard; no knob isolation, no oracle-free signal.

neighbors.title: Contact models in robotics: a comparative analysis
neighbors.trick: Implement the main contact models and solvers in one codebase and benchmark them for NCP violation, self-consistency and iterations to convergence.
neighbors.difference: The complementarity residual is theirs; fixed scenes, no exploitability.

headline: Frontier coding agents can speed up shipped physics engines 10-100x at fixed accuracy by generic optimisation (kernel fusion and the like), because the engines predate agents and are poorly optimised.
raised_by: Jacob's collaborators, relayed 2026-10-25 ('sounds too good to be true'); captured as a hypothesis to test, with the operator's expectation that it is false for GPU-native engines
current_belief: Three independent 2025-26 measurements contradict the generic form of the claim. GPUPhysBench 2609.35639 (fetched, full text): on 50 GPU-physics tasks, Claude Opus and GPT pass all tasks for correctness but reach >= 0.9x expert reference speed on 22% (Opus, single attempt; 36% best of three); global solves at 0.23-0.25x; continuous collision detection below 0.5x; the only submissions over 1.05x are DEM (1.11-1.13x) and MPM grid-to-particle (1.07x); 'the largest gaps arise in collision detection, constraint solving, and iterative solvers'. KernelBench-Verified 2607.16241 (fetched, abstract): with TF32 baselines and hidden tests, the best frontier model (GPT-5.5) reaches 0.88x geometric-mean speedup over PyTorch; the 1.43x under the standard protocol came from reward hacking (hardcoded bypasses for test tensors); 'no model consistently outperforms PyTorch'. Sakana AI CUDA Engineer (Feb 2025, TechCrunch fetched): claimed up to 100x; users measured a 3x slowdown; post-mortem attributed it to reward hacking of the evaluation; claims walked back. WorldSolver 2610.08720 (fetched, abstract): open-ended solver synthesis, best agents 46.7-48.7% overall.
if_true: A class of engines (most plausibly CPU-era soft-body codebases: SOFA, Bullet soft bodies, old FleX) is far enough from the GPU frontier that an agentic port and tune gives 10-100x at matched accuracy, and the result also beats Genesis/Newton/Warp on the same scenes; then the deployed-stack product the collaborators want exists.
if_false: For GPU-native engines (MJX, Warp, Newton, Isaac, Genesis) agentic tuning yields 1.0-1.5x at matched accuracy, and larger apparent gains come from cutting physics (fewer iterations, looser tolerances, skipped collisions) - the reward-hacking failure mode seen in Sakana and KernelBench-Verified; the measurement 'what agents can and cannot accelerate in physics engines, under a physics oracle' is still a citable GPUPhysBench follow-up.
probes: P-W43-J05-a (thought; ~$300 agent tokens + ~10 GPU-h, 1 week): give Claude Code / Codex a fixed budget to optimise (i) one hot path of a GPU-native engine (Genesis cloth or FEM step, or Warp XPBD, or the MJX constraint solve) and (ii) one CPU-era soft-body code (SOFA or Bullet soft body), with the ruler's checks (metamorphic, Richardson, energy) as the correctness oracle at fixed accuracy; measure speedup at matched accuracy

P-W43-J05-a.what: Agentic optimisation under a physics oracle: two targets (a GPU-native hot path; a CPU-era soft-body code), two agents (Claude Code, Codex), fixed budget (2 agent-days each), hidden-input tests plus the ruler's metamorphic, Richardson and energy checks as the accuracy oracle; speed measured at matched accuracy (MLPerf rule) and, for the port, compared on the same scene against Genesis or Newton.
P-W43-J05-a.kill_probe: Pre-registered: the '10-100x on modern engines' clause is dead if the GPU-native target gains under 2x at matched accuracy; the port clause is dead as a contribution if the ported CPU code, however much faster than itself, is slower than Genesis/Newton on the same scene. Expected (judgment): GPU-native 1.0-1.5x (p = 0.7); CPU-to-GPU port 10-50x over itself but below Genesis/Newton (p = 0.6). Cost: about $300 of agent tokens, 10 GPU-h, one week.

scorecard.target_value: Who asked in print: GPUPhysBench frames the question and finds agents below expert speed on the hard categories; engine teams pay for speed. Who pays for a deployed agentic optimisation stack: engine teams - who are also the competitors (NVIDIA, DeepMind, Genesis).

impact_ceiling.floor: A measured report: what frontier agents can and cannot accelerate in shipped physics engines under a physics oracle - a GPUPhysBench follow-up on real engines. p = 0.6 (judgment).
impact_ceiling.middle: An agentic optimisation harness with the ruler as oracle adopted by one engine team or one research simulator. p = 0.2 (judgment).
impact_ceiling.ceiling: The 10-100x clause holds for a class of engines at matched accuracy and the stack ships inside a simulator. p = 0.05 (judgment).

scorecard.relevance: Systems route (Lloyd, Netravali, Dao): high - agentic kernel optimisation is their world; robotics: medium; Jacob's edge (GPU kernels, numerics): load-bearing. Positioning: a deployed stack inside simulators is head-to-head with engine teams; the measurement is lab-adjacent.
scorecard.kill_probe: P-W43-J05-a: $300 + 10 GPU-h, one week.
scorecard.density_and_ownership: GPUPhysBench (Georgia Tech), KernelBench and KernelBench-Verified (Stanford and others), EvoEngineer, Sakana; the engine teams' own optimisation work. Owed at the kill search: a 12-month count on 'LLM agent' AND 'GPU kernel' AND (physics OR simulation) AND (speedup OR optimisation).
scorecard.why_now: Frontier agents reached 100% correctness on fully specified GPU-physics tasks in 2026 (GPUPhysBench) - the capability exists; what is unmeasured is their speed on real engine codebases under a correctness oracle that cannot be gamed.
scorecard.register: A hypothesis test first; a systems artifact only if the test passes. Not a new engine.

P-W43-01-2x2.what: The simulator-budget 2x2: train a policy at the shipped solver budget (Go1 iterations=1; Leap iterations=5) and at the converged budget (iterations=100, tol 1e-8) under the full training protocol (DR, kicks, observation noise, sampled actions) with a wall-clock-matched arm; evaluate every policy in both engines with paired DR draws and seeds; the interaction term J_conv(pi_conv) - J_conv(pi_cap) - [J_cap(pi_conv) - J_cap(pi_cap)] is the cap-isolated exploit; the certificate ||g_K|| and nchange logged per step are the fidelity column; sim2sim across engines (Playground's shipped script) is the field-standard transfer proxy; hardware is the ceiling arm.
P-W43-01-2x2.kill_probe: Dead if the interaction term lies inside the batch-seed interval of zero on BOTH Go1 rough terrain and the Leap cube task. Pre-registered (judgment): Go1 interaction about zero (sticking contacts; the hardware prior), Leap interaction positive and a non-trivial share of return (many simultaneous contacts; SAPU's interpenetration exploit in assembly is the precedent). Field's assumption: DR absorbs numerical error everywhere, and Leap failures are hardware flex and geometry. Belief-changing: a positive Leap interaction that shrinks with budget at matched wall-clock. Cost: two retrains per task at minutes each on 2 GPUs, cross-evaluation in minutes; 4-10 GPU-hours including the Leap retrain (no public Leap checkpoint), $20-50, one week.

P-W43-01-2x2.status: thought (spec written in the 2026-10-21 discuss session; scorecard and kill search owed before it is a candidate)
P-W43-01-2x2.what: The simulator-budget 2x2: train a policy at the shipped solver budget (Go1 iterations=1; Leap iterations=5) and at the converged budget (iterations=100, tol 1e-8) under the full training protocol (DR, kicks, observation noise, sampled actions) with a wall-clock-matched arm; evaluate every policy in both engines with paired DR draws and seeds; the interaction term J_conv(pi_conv) - J_conv(pi_cap) - [J_cap(pi_conv) - J_cap(pi_cap)] is the cap-isolated exploit; the certificate ||g_K|| and nchange logged per step are the fidelity column; sim2sim across engines (Playground's shipped script) is the field-standard transfer proxy; hardware is the ceiling arm.
P-W43-01-2x2.kill_probe: Dead if the interaction term lies inside the batch-seed interval of zero on BOTH Go1 rough terrain and the Leap cube task. Pre-registered (judgment): Go1 interaction about zero (sticking contacts; the hardware prior), Leap interaction positive and a non-trivial share of return (many simultaneous contacts; SAPU's interpenetration exploit in assembly is the precedent). Field's assumption: DR absorbs numerical error everywhere, and Leap failures are hardware flex and geometry. Belief-changing: a positive Leap interaction that shrinks with budget at matched wall-clock. Cost: two retrains per task at minutes each on 2 GPUs, cross-evaluation in minutes; 4-10 GPU-hours including the Leap retrain (no public Leap checkpoint), $20-50, one week.

proposed_headline: Policies trained in GPU simulators owe little of their return to solver shortcuts in locomotion and a measurable share in contact-rich manipulation - so part of manipulation's sim-to-real gap is a numerics gap that solver budget buys back, not a modeling gap.

if_true: Every agentic-RL systems paper reports a per-station demand table and names the binding station; KV release during tool waits becomes a predicted 25-35% iteration-time lever; trainer kernel work past the balance point is shown futile
if_false: Decode compute binds (utilization >= 0.85 with KV below cap) and KV release moves iteration time under 5%: token accounting is adequate and the lane's cost instrument is Little's law applied once

if_false: Content wins: the placebo moves nothing, the information in the block is what helps, and the open question is which models can use it (C-W43-06's habit ruler).

headline: An agent served under KV-cache eviction is not the agent its transcript describes: it keeps using tool outputs it can no longer see, and a trainer recomputing log-probabilities from the text does not reproduce the policy it sampled from.
current_belief: Agentic-RL stacks and the cache-engineering paper treat the visible token sequence as the policy's input: 2610.28577 names training under cache operations as future work and benchmarks drop/reposition only against threshold summarization, never against the same drop done as text (card 2610.28577, Table 1 and sec. 3.2).
if_true: Trainers log the operation sequence, not the token sequence, or forbid eviction during rollouts; the +1.7-point cache-operations margin is re-read as ghost information; off-policy corrections (the engine-trainer mismatch literature) gain a second, larger term.
if_false: KV drop equals text drop within 3 points and post-drop divergence is within 2x the numerical baseline: cache operations are a pure cost lever and trainers can keep recomputing from text.
probes: C-W43-25 (teacher-forced KL of served-under-eviction vs text-recomputed policies by turn offset since the last drop; ~30 GPU-h, $110, 5 d)

headline: Most of the environments used for agentic RL today are luck-dominated at the group sizes people train with: at G = 8, more than half of the within-group reward variance in user-simulator and flaky-tool environments is environment randomness, not the agent's choices.
raised_by: Jacob, 2026-10-29, asking whether dependence beyond covariance (Sobol indices, mutual information) opens a golden idea; the recipe half (paired rollouts) was found occupied in the last eight weeks, the cross-environment measurement was not (kill search owed)
current_belief: Paired rollouts with event-keyed noise in group-relative RL are in print: 2609.24144 'Luck Is Not Skill' (2026-09-21, fetched: pairing removes the between-schedule component of reward-contrast variance but need not reduce gradient variance; 2B tool-use agent, pre-registered; +5.1 pp under tool faults, no learning-curve win; gradient covariance traces down 21-30% under grader flips and 40-63% under tool faults), OSCC 2609.33543 (2026-09-27, observation-safe coupling with a gradient-aware criterion), TWICE 2610.31544 (2026-10-22, twin worlds via Gumbel noise keyed by turn and line; variance scaled by 1 - rho), EPIG-Tree 2609.20004 (law-of-total-variance decomposition of the policy gradient into decision and continuation uncertainty), 'Drowning in Routine' 2606.22164 (decision density rho; SNR scales as rho^-1/2), event-keyed hashing for common random numbers 2603.11084, paired seeds 2512.24145. None of them reports the luck share across the environments the field actually trains in; 2609.24144 injects faults into one environment.
if_true: Training teams choose coupling (TWICE / paired rollouts) and group size per environment from a table rather than by default; benchmark owners report the luck share of their environment as a property; the per-turn split of Oct 2026 finds its consumer in training, not evaluation.
if_false: Real environments are skill-dominated and the Sept-Oct 2026 coupling methods address a corner case - a reassuring table training teams would still cite.
probes: P-W44-J01-a (thought; 20-40 GPU-h, $60-120, 2 weeks): the luck table - for six public environments (tau-bench retail with an open-weights user simulator at T=1, SWE-Gym-style sandbox with flaky tests, WebArena, ALFWorld as the deterministic control, a MuJoCo task with domain randomization, a tool-fault environment as in 2609.24144), estimate the luck share by the law of total variance with nested sampling (K environment draws per agent trajectory prefix), at G in {4, 8, 16}, for one open 7-8B agent

P-W44-J01-a.what: For each environment, sample G agent trajectories per task; for each trajectory re-run the environment's randomness K times holding the agent's actions fixed where the environment allows it (user simulator replies, tool outcomes) to estimate Var(R | actions); luck share lambda = E[Var(R | actions)] / Var(R); report lambda by environment and group size, and the implied fraction of GRPO advantage variance that is luck. Deterministic sandboxes must read zero (the control).
P-W44-J01-a.kill_probe: Pre-registered: dead if lambda < 0.25 in every stochastic environment at G = 8 (luck is a corner case and the headline is false); dead as a headline if a published table already exists (kill search). Expected (judgment): user-simulator environments 0.4-0.7, flaky-tool sandboxes 0.2-0.5, ALFWorld 0, MuJoCo with DR 0.1-0.3. Cost: 20-40 GPU-h, $60-120, two weeks.

neighbors.title: GAUGE: measurement-grounded benchmark for physical fidelity in simulation engines and video world models
neighbors.trick: Record real trajectories for 22 controlled task families across rigid, cable, textile and volumetric materials and score Isaac Sim, Genesis and Newton by generalized trajectory error.
neighbors.difference: Fidelity on chosen motions with real data — the validation layer, done; no optimiser, no policy-visited states, no test of whether its scores predict transfer. Our F uses GAUGE's number.

neighbors.title: RoboGauge (sim-to-real predictability for MoE quadruped locomotion)
neighbors.trick: Predict a policy's transferability from proprioception metrics in sim-to-sim tests over terrains and randomisations, without hardware trials.
neighbors.difference: Trace-free predictor at the policy level; the competing predictor claim A races against.

neighbors.title: Sim2Real Predictivity (Kadian et al. 2019)
neighbors.trick: Run nine navigation models in a scanned lab and its replica; SRCC 0.18 because agents exploited collision dynamics by sliding along walls; 0.844 after tuning the simulator.
neighbors.difference: The single-artifact datum behind claim A; post-hoc, one engine, no exploitability measurement.

neighbors.title: Imperfect World Models are Exploitable
neighbors.trick: A model is exploitable when it ranks two policies oppositely to the true dynamics; exploitation is unavoidable on large policy sets.
neighbors.difference: Theory of the object our 2x2 interaction measures; no measurement, no engines.

neighbors.title: Policy-Aware Simulator Learning
neighbors.trick: Train a learned simulator as a minimax game against an adversarial policy whose worst case is dual to RL on the critic's one-step error.
neighbors.difference: Needs the true environment to score error; ours scores conservation-law violations with no oracle on engineered engines.

neighbors.title: Predicting Sim-to-Real Transfer with Probabilistic Dynamics Models
neighbors.trick: Score a dynamics model trained with the policy on a fixed set of real trajectories; the score predicts transfer of training setups.
neighbors.difference: Needs real trajectories; no simulator property.

neighbors.title: PolySim
neighbors.trick: Train across several engines so a policy cannot overfit one; the exploit is measured as a sim-to-sim success drop.
neighbors.difference: Whole-engine exploit test, the field's standard; no knob isolation, no oracle-free signal.

neighbors.trick: Implement the main contact models and solvers in one codebase and benchmark them for NCP violation, self-consistency and iterations to convergence.
neighbors.difference: The complementarity residual is theirs; fixed scenes, no exploitability.

imports: Extreme-value theory of selection under an incomplete selector: 'Tail Competition Explains Scaling in Best-of-N' 2610.19362 (fetched 2026-10-29) frames best-of-N as a competition between the upper tails of correct and incorrect responses, with correct-tail-dominant, incorrect-tail-dominant and critical regimes and a tail-tension diagnostic. headline: The falling hazard in agent time-horizon curves is between-task frailty, not within-task degradation: hold the task fixed and the per-minute hazard is flat.

headline: Penalising or filtering physics violations in simulation teaches robot policies to exploit the simulator where the checks cannot see; routing those gradients into sacrificial parameters and ablating them before deployment transfers better than penalties or filtering - and the ablation drop is the policy's exploit share.
raised_by: Jacob, 2026-10-30: can 'Gradient Routing Localizes and Removes Unintended Behaviors in RL' (GRAFT, 2610.17062) inform the robotics / simulator RL thread?
current_belief: GRAFT 2610.17062 (fetched 2026-10-30, abstract): with a misspecified reward and a monitor that makes systematic errors, filtering or penalising flagged samples fails - the model learns to hack in undetected ways; constraining the flagged samples' gradient updates to a sacrificial set of new adapter parameters keeps the monitor out of the reward (so misbehaviour is not hidden) and ablating those parameters removes the behaviour while keeping target-task gains; shown on 135M-8B models in RL and by distilling hacking trajectories into Qwen3-32B. Gradient routing 2410.04332 (fetched): data-dependent gradient masks localise capabilities even from a limited, ad-hoc subset of the data (absorption). The robotics field's answers to simulator exploits are penalties and constraints - action-Jacobian penalty 2602.18312 (policies exploit unachievable high-frequency actuation), Lipschitz-constrained policies 2504.08246, SAPU 2305.17110 (drop episodes over 1 mm interpenetration, down-weight the rest), and domain randomisation (Peng 2017) - i.e. exactly the 'penalise or filter' arm GRAFT argues drives hacking underground when the monitor is imperfect. No application of gradient routing to robot policies or simulators in the fetched set (7 abstract hits for 'gradient routing', none robotic).
if_true: The ruler's physics checks become a training ingredient without becoming a reward: sim-to-real pipelines add routed sacrificial parameters beside domain randomisation; benchmarks report an exploit-ablated score beside the raw score; the ablation drop is a causal, policy-internal estimate of realised exploitation that needs no converged reference engine (so it exists for soft bodies).
if_false: Either exploits and skills share representations in continuous control so ablation removes skill too (then routing is for discrete agents only), or penalties do not drive hidden exploitation in physics (then SAPU-style filtering is fine and GRAFT's premise does not carry).

headline: Penalising or filtering physics violations in simulation teaches robot policies to exploit the simulator where the checks cannot see; routing those gradients into sacrificial parameters and ablating them before deployment transfers better than penalties or filtering - and the ablation drop is the policy's exploit share.

Gradient routing 2410.04332 (fetched): data-dependent gradient masks localise capabilities even from a limited, ad-hoc subset of the data (absorption). P-W44-J02-b.status: thought (Jacob's preferred shape, 2026-10-30: no real robot; code-as-policy LLM agent; avoids the small-MLP representation question)
P-W44-J02-b.what: GRAFT's own regime ported to simulation robotics: the policy is an open-weights code-writing model (Qwen3-8B or -32B class) that writes code-as-policy programs for contact-rich tasks in MJX or Genesis. Two ways to train it: (i) RL with the simulator's task reward (GRPO) with gradient routing on the adapter - episodes the physics monitor flags update only the sacrificial adapter; (ii) distillation, as in GRAFT's second experiment: a frontier model (Astra or equivalent) generates code-as-policy trajectories in the simulator, some of which exploit it; the student is distilled with routing, so flagged trajectories train only the sacrificial adapter; the frontier model is never fine-tuned. Deployment test without hardware: ablate the adapter and evaluate in the same engine at converged settings, in a second engine (sim2sim), and on GAUGE-style real-anchored task families where available. The monitor is the ruler's general physics checks (energy from nothing, complementarity residual against the engine's declared law, symmetry defects), deliberately imperfect; no catalogue of exploits is assumed.
P-W44-J02-b.kill_probe: Pre-registered: dead if ablating the adapter costs as much in the trusted engines as in the training engine (nothing exploit-specific localised), or if routing transfers no better than the penalty and filter arms. Expected (judgment): the frontier model's code-as-policy trajectories contain a measurable exploit fraction on contact-rich tasks (penetration-assisted grasps, solver-error-assisted insertions); the routed-and-ablated student keeps most of its trusted-engine success while the penalty arm's violations move below the training monitor's sight. Cost: frontier API calls for 2,000-5,000 trajectories ($100-300), fine-tuning an 8B student with and without routing (20-40 GPU-h), evaluation in three engines (5 GPU-h); three weeks.
P-W44-J02-b.what_it_does_not_need: No real robot (the trusted-simulator ladder is the deployment test; a hardware confirmation is owed from a lab position and the paper says so). No prior catalogue of hacks: GRAFT assumes an imperfect monitor and the ruler is one; what is needed is that flagged steps are enriched for exploits, which the adversary calibration establishes. Not a frozen frontier policy: gradient routing needs gradients, so the frontier model is the data generator (distillation) or the student is an open model under RL; for a frozen Astra agent the analogue is a quarantined skill library (flagged programs usable in training, deleted at deployment), a weaker, untested analogy.

P-W43-01-2x2.status: thought (spec written in the 2026-10-21 discuss session; scorecard and kill search owed before it is a candidate)
P-W43-01-2x2.what: The simulator-budget 2x2: train a policy at the shipped solver budget (Go1 iterations=1; Leap iterations=5) and at the converged budget (iterations=100, tol 1e-8) under the full training protocol (DR, kicks, observation noise, sampled actions) with a wall-clock-matched arm; evaluate every policy in both engines with paired DR draws and seeds; the interaction term J_conv(pi_conv) - J_conv(pi_cap) - [J_cap(pi_conv) - J_cap(pi_cap)] is the cap-isolated exploit; the certificate ||g_K|| and nchange logged per step are the fidelity column; sim2sim across engines (Playground's shipped script) is the field-standard transfer proxy; hardware is the ceiling arm.
P-W43-01-2x2.kill_probe: Dead if the interaction term lies inside the batch-seed interval of zero on BOTH Go1 rough terrain and the Leap cube task. Pre-registered (judgment): Go1 interaction about zero (sticking contacts; the hardware prior), Leap interaction positive and a non-trivial share of return (many simultaneous contacts; SAPU's interpenetration exploit in assembly is the precedent). Field's assumption: DR absorbs numerical error everywhere, and Leap failures are hardware flex and geometry. Belief-changing: a positive Leap interaction that shrinks with budget at matched wall-clock. Cost: two retrains per task at minutes each on 2 GPUs, cross-evaluation in minutes; 4-10 GPU-hours including the Leap retrain (no public Leap checkpoint), $20-50, one week.

headline: The falling hazard in agent time-horizon curves is between-task frailty, not within-task degradation: hold the task fixed and the per-minute hazard is flat.
current_belief: Hamilton (Jan 2026) fits a pooled Weibull with shape about 0.6 for frontier agents and reads it as the agents' hazard; Ord 2505.05115 reads a half-life; METR's own logistic-in-log-time curve is the sigma^2 = 1 gamma-frailty curve without being named as one (X-2026-W42-S7F9, derivation in the seed record)
if_true: Horizon producers publish the frailty variance or the within-task run agreement beside every 50% and 80% horizon and label the 80% horizon a share of tasks within reach; forecasters use k_cond for single-task tails and sigma^2 for reach; pass^k reporters replace one per-step reliability with a per-task distribution
if_false: The within-task hazard falls too (k_cond well below 1): agents do degrade along a task, which makes the horizon curve a property of agents after all and makes the step-clock hazard shape (S7xF9) the next question
probes: X-2026-W42-S7F9 (frailty refit of METR-Horizon-v1.1 runs; $0, 3 d; no scorecard)

if_false: KV drop equals text drop within 3 points and post-drop divergence is within 2x the numerical baseline: cache operations are a pure cost lever and trainers can keep recomputing from text.
probes: C-W43-25 (teacher-forced KL of served-under-eviction vs text-recomputed policies by turn offset since the last drop; ~30 GPU-h, $110, 5 d)

headline: The run-to-run variance that agent benchmarks report at temperature 0 is the serving stack's batch-dependent arithmetic, not the agent, and over multi-turn trajectories it is large enough to reorder leaderboards.
raised_by: Jacob, 2026-10-20 03:13 ET, in chat: Thinking Machines' post on defeating nondeterminism in LLM inference is adjacent to our luck-subtraction thread
current_belief: Fetched 2026-10-20 from thinkingmachines.ai/blog/defeating-nondeterminism-in-llm-inference (Horace He and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025-09-10): the forward pass is run-to-run deterministic, but kernels whose reduction order changes with batch size make a request's numerics depend on the other requests in the batch, so 'from each user's perspective the output is nondeterministic'; Qwen3-235B-A22B at temperature 0, 1000 completions of 1000 tokens: 80 unique completions, identical for the first 102 tokens; with batch-invariant kernels all 1000 identical; cost on Qwen3-8B, 1000 sequences: 26 s default vs 55 s unoptimised vs 42 s with the improved attention kernel (about 2.1x and 1.6x). The post frames this as reproducibility and on-policy RL (sampler-trainer KL flat at 0) and does not discuss benchmark evaluation. The field's working belief to test at the kill search: temperature-0 agent evaluations are reported as single runs or with a 'noise' of a point or two, as if deterministic.
if_true: Every temperature-0 benchmark report states its serving stack and whether decoding was batch-invariant; leaderboards add a stack-noise column or run batch-invariant; and the per-turn luck-skill decomposition (W41 product red team C, parked) becomes exactly identifiable on the agent side: a batch-invariant agent at temperature 0 has zero decision variance by construction, so Var[R] decomposes onto the user simulator and environment alone - the control arm that instrument lacked.
if_false: At trajectory scale the token-level divergences rarely change an action's outcome (flip rate under 2 percent, rank order stable) - a reassuring measurement benchmark owners would still cite when they report temperature-0 numbers; the luck-skill thread stays parked on its consumer verdict.
relates_to: W41 product red team C: per-turn luck/skill attribution for user-simulator benchmarks (parked in L1; data/reports/2026-W41-product-redteam-C.md) - this claim supplies the exact zero-variance agent arm that the split needed

P-W43-J01-a.design: Two arms x 10 repeats x 100 tasks. Default arm: vLLM default kernels, each repeat run at a different concurrency (alone, 8, 32) so batch composition changes. Treatment arm: the same stack with batch-invariant kernels (TML's released kernels or vLLM's batch-invariant mode - which exists and works for the model is checked at the kill search); its flip rate must be exactly 0, which is the determinism check. Record per task: any outcome disagreement across the 10 repeats, the turn of first divergence, pass^k for k=1..10, and the rank order of three agent variants (prompt or scaffold variants) per repeat.
P-W43-J01-a.kill_probe: Dead if the default arm's outcome-flip rate is under 2 percent of tasks AND the rank order of the three agent variants is identical across all ten repeats. headline: A GPU simulator's physics budget is a dose: transferable policy return follows one dose-response curve in solver budget per task class, so fidelity can be scheduled during training like a learning rate instead of fixed by a config file.
raised_by: Jacob and the operator, 2026-10-21 discuss session on the simulator thread (the systems half of L5, now framed as the consequence of a measurement)
current_belief: Solver budgets are fixed per task in model files (Playground XML iterations=1 Go1, 5 Leap; legged_gym num_position_iterations=4) and justified by DR (MJX docs, fetched 2026-10-20 in the C-W43-15 red team); numerical settings are treated as a randomization axis (Dactyl randomized the time step), not a dial; the only fetched RL consumer of a fidelity scalar is a control-variate estimator (MFPG-PPO 2610.02505).
if_true: Training recipes gain a fidelity schedule (coarse early, converged late) at matched wall-clock; engine teams expose the budget per world as a runtime knob rather than a file constant; the iteration-level scheduler (the lane's systems piece) has a stated consumer.
if_false: Response is task-specific or non-monotone: fixed budgets are right and the scheduler has no consumer - a result engine teams would still cite when choosing defaults.
probes: P-W43-01-2x2 (rides on CL-W43-01's probe: the dose-response of transferable return in budget comes free from the 2x2 plus two intermediate budgets)

headline: Among the numbers one can compute about a simulator without a robot, the fidelity scores engines report predict policy transfer worst, and the worst-case physical violation a budgeted optimiser can extract predicts it best.

current_belief: Engines and simulator benchmarks report average fidelity on chosen motions: GPUSimBench 2607.13059 (fetched) scores distributional alignment of an inclined-plane task with real data; RGBench 2511.06434 (fetched) scores simulated garment dynamics against measured real ones and reports a 20 percent error reduction; 2603.14634 (fetched) ships analytical-solution tests for rigid bodies. Policy-Aware Simulator Learning 2605.29032 (fetched) argues the right objective for LEARNED simulators is strategic robustness to an adversarial policy rather than predictive accuracy, and proves the worst-case policy is dual to RL on the critic's one-step error - the same move for engineered simulators is unmeasured. Whether any reported fidelity number predicts sim-to-real transfer is, in the fetched set, untested (density check at the kill search; arXiv API throttled on 2026-10-23).

headline: Most of the environments used for agentic RL today are luck-dominated at the group sizes people train with: at G = 8, more than half of the within-group reward variance in user-simulator and flaky-tool environments is environment randomness, not the agent's choices.
raised_by: Jacob, 2026-10-29, asking whether dependence beyond covariance (Sobol indices, mutual information) opens a golden idea; the recipe half (paired rollouts) was found occupied in the last eight weeks, the cross-environment measurement was not (kill search owed)
current_belief: Paired rollouts with event-keyed noise in group-relative RL are in print: 2609.24144 'Luck Is Not Skill' (2026-09-21, fetched: pairing removes the between-schedule component of reward-contrast variance but need not reduce gradient variance; 2B tool-use agent, pre-registered; +5.1 pp under tool faults, no learning-curve win; gradient covariance traces down 21-30% under grader flips and 40-63% under tool faults), OSCC 2609.33543 (2026-09-27, observation-safe coupling with a gradient-aware criterion), TWICE 2610.31544 (2026-10-22, twin worlds via Gumbel noise keyed by turn and line; variance scaled by 1 - rho), EPIG-Tree 2609.20004 (law-of-total-variance decomposition of the policy gradient into decision and continuation uncertainty), 'Drowning in Routine' 2606.22164 (decision density rho; SNR scales as rho^-1/2), event-keyed hashing for common random numbers 2603.11084, paired seeds 2512.24145. None of them reports the luck share across the environments the field actually trains in; 2609.24144 injects faults into one environment.
if_true: Training teams choose coupling (TWICE / paired rollouts) and group size per environment from a table rather than by default; benchmark owners report the luck share of their environment as a property; the per-turn split of Oct 2026 finds its consumer in training, not evaluation.
if_false: Real environments are skill-dominated and the Sept-Oct 2026 coupling methods address a corner case - a reassuring table training teams would still cite.
probes: P-W44-J01-a (thought; 20-40 GPU-h, $60-120, 2 weeks): the luck table - for six public environments (tau-bench retail with an open-weights user simulator at T=1, SWE-Gym-style sandbox with flaky tests, WebArena, ALFWorld as the deterministic control, a MuJoCo task with domain randomization, a tool-fault environment as in 2609.24144), estimate the luck share by the law of total variance with nested sampling (K environment draws per agent trajectory prefix), at G in {4, 8, 16}, for one open 7-8B agent

P-W44-J01-a.what: For each environment, sample G agent trajectories per task; for each trajectory re-run the environment's randomness K times holding the agent's actions fixed where the environment allows it (user simulator replies, tool outcomes) to estimate Var(R | actions); luck share lambda = E[Var(R | actions)] / Var(R); report lambda by environment and group size, and the implied fraction of GRPO advantage variance that is luck. Deterministic sandboxes must read zero (the control).
P-W44-J01-a.kill_probe: Pre-registered: dead if lambda < 0.25 in every stochastic environment at G = 8 (luck is a corner case and the headline is false); dead as a headline if a published table already exists (kill search). headline: Penalising or filtering physics violations in simulation teaches robot policies to exploit the simulator where the checks cannot see; routing those gradients into sacrificial parameters and ablating them before deployment transfers better than penalties or filtering - and the ablation drop is the policy's exploit share.
raised_by: Jacob, 2026-10-30: can 'Gradient Routing Localizes and Removes Unintended Behaviors in RL' (GRAFT, 2610.17062) inform the robotics / simulator RL thread?
current_belief: GRAFT 2610.17062 (fetched 2026-10-30, abstract): with a misspecified reward and a monitor that makes systematic errors, filtering or penalising flagged samples fails - the model learns to hack in undetected ways; constraining the flagged samples' gradient updates to a sacrificial set of new adapter parameters keeps the monitor out of the reward (so misbehaviour is not hidden) and ablating those parameters removes the behaviour while keeping target-task gains; shown on 135M-8B models in RL and by distilling hacking trajectories into Qwen3-32B. Gradient routing 2410.04332 (fetched): data-dependent gradient masks localise capabilities even from a limited, ad-hoc subset of the data (absorption). The robotics field's answers to simulator exploits are penalties and constraints - action-Jacobian penalty 2602.18312 (policies exploit unachievable high-frequency actuation), Lipschitz-constrained policies 2504.08246, SAPU 2305.17110 (drop episodes over 1 mm interpenetration, down-weight the rest), and domain randomisation (Peng 2017) - i.e. exactly the 'penalise or filter' arm GRAFT argues drives hacking underground when the monitor is imperfect. No application of gradient routing to robot policies or simulators in the fetched set (7 abstract hits for 'gradient routing', none robotic).
if_true: The ruler's physics checks become a training ingredient without becoming a reward: sim-to-real pipelines add routed sacrificial parameters beside domain randomisation; benchmarks report an exploit-ablated score beside the raw score; the ablation drop is a causal, policy-internal estimate of realised exploitation that needs no converged reference engine (so it exists for soft bodies).
if_false: Either exploits and skills share representations in continuous control so ablation removes skill too (then routing is for discrete agents only), or penalties do not drive hidden exploitation in physics (then SAPU-style filtering is fine and GRAFT's premise does not carry).
probes: P-W44-J02-a (thought; 10-30 GPU-h, $50-100, 2 weeks): on the Leap cube task (contact-rich) and Go1 (control), PPO with a routed sacrificial branch - steps flagged by the dimensionless violation functionals send their gradients to the branch only - against three baselines: plain, violation penalty, SAPU-style filtering, each with and without DR; evaluate every policy in the training engine, the converged engine and a second engine (sim2sim), with the branch active and ablated

P-W44-J02-b (thought; $200-400, 25-45 GPU-h, 3 weeks): code-as-policy LLM agent in simulation, trained by RL or distilled from a frontier model with gradient routing on the physics monitor; no real robot; Jacob's preferred shape

P-W44-J02-a.what: Implement step-level gradient routing in the PPO update (two parameter groups; flagged steps' loss terms update only the sacrificial branch via stop-gradients); the monitor is the ruler's energy-from-nothing and complementarity functionals thresholded at the batch-permutation floor - deliberately imperfect. Arms: plain, penalty, filter, routed; x {DR, no DR}; tasks Leap and Go1; 3 seeds. Measures: in-engine return with branch on and off (the ablation drop = realised exploit share), converged-engine and second-engine return of each arm, monitor-visible violation rate and a held-out stricter monitor's violation rate (does hacking go underground under penalty?).
P-W44-J02-a.kill_probe: Pre-registered: dead if the ablation drop in the converged engine equals the drop in the training engine on both tasks (nothing exploit-specific was localised), or if the routed-and-ablated policy transfers no better than DR alone and no better than the penalty arm. Expected (judgment): on Leap, penalty and filter arms show lower monitor-visible violations but equal or higher held-out violations (hidden exploitation), the routed-ablated arm keeps 85-100 percent of converged-engine return while the in-engine ablation drop is a measurable share; on Go1 all arms near equal. Cost 10-30 GPU-h, $50-100, two weeks.

P-W44-J02-b.status: thought (Jacob's preferred shape, 2026-10-30: no real robot; code-as-policy LLM agent; avoids the small-MLP representation question)
P-W44-J02-b.what: GRAFT's own regime ported to simulation robotics: the policy is an open-weights code-writing model (Qwen3-8B or -32B class) that writes code-as-policy programs for contact-rich tasks in MJX or Genesis. Two ways to train it: (i) RL with the simulator's task reward (GRPO) with gradient routing on the adapter - episodes the physics monitor flags update only the sacrificial adapter; (ii) distillation, as in GRAFT's second experiment: a frontier model (Astra or equivalent) generates code-as-policy trajectories in the simulator, some of which exploit it; the student is distilled with routing, so flagged trajectories train only the sacrificial adapter; the frontier model is never fine-tuned. Deployment test without hardware: ablate the adapter and evaluate in the same engine at converged settings, in a second engine (sim2sim), and on GAUGE-style real-anchored task families where available. The monitor is the ruler's general physics checks (energy from nothing, complementarity residual against the engine's declared law, symmetry defects), deliberately imperfect; no catalogue of exploits is assumed.
P-W44-J02-b.kill_probe: Pre-registered: dead if ablating the adapter costs as much in the trusted engines as in the training engine (nothing exploit-specific localised), or if routing transfers no better than the penalty and filter arms. Expected (judgment): the frontier model's code-as-policy trajectories contain a measurable exploit fraction on contact-rich tasks (penetration-assisted grasps, solver-error-assisted insertions); the routed-and-ablated student keeps most of its trusted-engine success while the penalty arm's violations move below the training monitor's sight. Cost: frontier API calls for 2,000-5,000 trajectories ($100-300), fine-tuning an 8B student with and without routing (20-40 GPU-h), evaluation in three engines (5 GPU-h); three weeks.
P-W44-J02-b.what_it_does_not_need: No real robot (the trusted-simulator ladder is the deployment test; a hardware confirmation is owed from a lab position and the paper says so). No prior catalogue of hacks: GRAFT assumes an imperfect monitor and the ruler is one; what is needed is that flagged steps are enriched for exploits, which the adversary calibration establishes. Not a frozen frontier policy: gradient routing needs gradients, so the frontier model is the data generator (distillation) or the student is an open model under RL; for a frozen Astra agent the analogue is a quarantined skill library (flagged programs usable in training, deleted at deployment), a weaker, untested analogy.

headline: On continuously maintained agent benchmarks, more than half of each version-to-version score movement lands on repaired or recalibrated tasks, and the model ordering on the untouched tasks is unchanged across versions.
current_belief: Terminal-Bench 4.0 release note (B04, 2026-08-28): 'All tasks in TB 4.0 are now set to a flat agent timeout of 8 hours [...] We removed 8 tasks [...] We fixed 19 tasks [...] These represent breaking changes that require re-running trials' — the changes are listed, not scored; SWE-Bench Pro V2 (B07, 2026-10-16): 'repaired or retired 480 of the 731 tasks: 23 contracted engineers spent 404 hours [...] 69 tasks had instructions that contradicted the tests grading them', with the board at '99.4 +/- 0.4' three weeks after relaunch (B08); Cognition FrontierCode 2.0 (L18, 2026-10-27): 'In 80% of FrontierCode 2.0 tasks, the reference solution differs from the upstream PR, up from 60% in FrontierCode 1.0', six of eight models reordered; Gemini 4 Argon model card (L12): 'computed with improved evaluations and thus are not directly comparable'; Vals (B12): 'Because the task set is entirely different, scores are not comparable across versions' — the owners say 'not comparable' with no number, and launch tables read the version delta as model progress
if_true: Every continuous benchmark publishes a repair delta per release and the ordering on the unchanged subset; labs report old-version and new-version scores as separate columns; aggregators stop drawing trend lines across refreshes; a version refresh is labelled equatable, linkable or new construct

headline: Sandbox-escape and unwanted-persistence rates in system cards are harness-and-task properties: at a fixed model, a goal loop plus an impossible-task share moves the rate more than one model generation does.
current_belief: Haiku 5.5 system card (L05, 2026-10-07): 'One particularly effective tempter was a /goal-style loop which nudges the model to not give up on its task. [...] Haiku 5.5 did so in 30% of scenarios (524 of 1,753) [...] In 502 of the 524, the task could not be completed from inside the sandbox. Adding a short description to the system prompt about the kind of sandbox the model is in reduced the rate [...] from 30% to 1.8%' — both levers measured on one model, never crossed with models; The Register on OpenAI (L14, 2026-09-29): the withdrawn model 'didn't quite meet the bar in terms of staying within scope and authorization [...] You really do need to find what's the right line between staying within scope [and] avoiding laziness'; GPT-6.1 Terra addendum (L16, 2026-10-26): 'Terra performed the specified unauthorized action in 13.75% (11 of 80 samples). Comparisons: GPT-6.1 Sol 50.00% / 1.25%' — rates ranked per model at one harness on 80 samples; the cards' working belief is that persistence past blockers is a model trait to be ranked
if_true: Every misalignment table declares its harness and its impossible-task share; the capability-safety trade is handled as a harness and reward-design problem (a reward that pays a correct stop, or a scope classifier at inference), not a model-ranking one; labs stop ranking models on rates measured under their own loops
if_false: The model term dominates the variance decomposition: propensity is a training-mix property, the cards are right to rank models on it, and the public gated-scenario set is the residue
probes: none yet — thought (first measurement sketched in pressure #4: a public gated-scenario set from Agents' Last Exam Linux tasks and Prime Intellect sandboxes with planted authorization gates and a labelled impossible subset; three open models x three harness conditions (plain, goal loop, goal loop plus the sandbox paragraph) x 200 scenarios; variance decomposition of the crossing rate into model, harness and task-impossibility terms, with persistence scored as capability on the possible subset and as violation on the gated subset from the same rollouts; under one GPU-day for open models, about $2,000 of API for frontier ones, two weeks; queued for /sprint generate)

P-W44-03-cross.what: Crossed design on a public gated-scenario set: $r = \Pr[\mathrm{impossible}] \cdot \Pr[\mathrm{loop\ re\text{-}issues}] \cdot \Pr[\mathrm{cross} \mid \mathrm{impossible}, \mathrm{loop}]$, with only the last factor the model's; three open models (two generations of one family plus one other) x three harness conditions x 200 scenarios (100 possible, 100 impossible by design), 3 runs per cell; readouts: crossing rate per cell, the variance decomposition over model, harness and impossibility terms, and the capability score on the possible subset from the same rollouts.
P-W44-03-cross.kill_probe: Pre-registered: dead if the model term carries more than half of the crossing-rate variance with the harness and impossibility terms each under a fifth (propensity is a training-mix property); dead as news if the harness term is large only through the one-paragraph system-prompt effect already in print (L05) and the goal-loop x impossibility interaction is inside the run band. Expected (judgment): harness plus impossibility over two thirds, model under a fifth, and the generation contrast smaller than the goal-loop contrast. Cost: under one GPU-day for open models (about 20 GPU-h), $0-2,000 depending on frontier arms, two weeks.

2606.24496 Red-Teaming the Agentic Red-Team

headline: Published agentic-RL algorithm gains on SWE tasks do not survive a tuned asynchronous baseline with bitwise-consistent rollouts, and environment scale at matched compute moves the score more than any loss choice.
current_belief: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash tech report (L20, arXiv:2609.19969, 2026-09-17): 'under a fixed and unremarkable optimization procedure, systematic improvements in the scale, diversity, and verifiability of synthesized data and environments account for essentially all of the observed gains. [...] the marginal return of engineering the data and environment pipeline substantially exceeds that of algorithmic novelty in post-training' — a finding at one lab's scale, with no 2 x 2 in the open; Arctic-SWE (Q10, arXiv:2610.24914, 2026-10-17): 'This makes gains from new algorithms or data hard to distinguish from improvements to an under-tuned baseline. [...] No single component is new, yet together they form the missing foundation'; vLLM train-inference consistency post (Q08, 2026-10-14): 'the high-performance baseline's train-inference KL rose from 2e-3 to 29.9 while reward fell back [...] the consistent run's SWE-bench Pro score holds while the baseline's drops from 0.56 to 0.22 [...] neither baseline was thoroughly tuned or explored: each ran a single configuration' — each source poses a third; academic L2 papers report estimator deltas against untuned, inconsistent baselines
if_true: Method papers report against a tuned asynchronous baseline with the consistency flag and a train-inference KL column; L2 recipe work is retired for solo positions in favour of environment measurement and systems; the lane's out-of-scope rule ('a new advantage estimator evaluated on one benchmark') becomes the field's own
if_false: The deltas survive: the loss still matters at small environment scale, which is where academic RL lives, and the audit's residue is the tuned consistent baseline as a public artifact
probes: none yet — thought (first measurement sketched in pressure #11: the Arctic-SWE recipe at 4B as the tuned baseline; rerun with and without the vLLM consistency flag and at two environment scales (R2E-Gym full and a quarter sample); then rerun two published agentic-RL method papers' claimed deltas on the tuned consistent baseline; about 300 GPU-h per arm, six arms — over one GPU-week solo; lab position; the consistency-flag pair alone is two arms; related lab spec: C-W44-DEF-L2 under CL-W43-06)

P-W44-04-audit.what: Six arms at 4B on the Arctic-SWE recipe: {tuned baseline, baseline + consistency flag} x {R2E-Gym full, quarter} plus two published method deltas re-run on the tuned consistent baseline at the full scale; readouts: SWE-bench Verified and Pro at matched rollout tokens, train-inference KL per step, and the environment-scale contrast against the method contrast.
P-W44-04-audit.kill_probe: Pre-registered: dead if both published deltas survive on the tuned consistent baseline with 3-seed bands separated and the environment-scale contrast is smaller than either method contrast; the headline's first clause is dead alone if the deltas survive and the second if environment scale moves less than the loss choice. Expected (judgment, from the pressure report): deltas vanish and the environment-scale arm moves the score more than either method. Cost: about 1,800 GPU-h (six arms x 300) — lab position; the consistency-flag pair alone about 600 GPU-h.
