headline: Model-written adversarial audits do not bound what an optimiser extracts from a simulator: in agent-built simulators that passed three audit rounds, a 600-episode search against the verifier makes at least one in twenty verified successes physically invalid.
current_belief: Gym-Anything for Robotics (2610.40565, 2026-10-29; card and candidate C-W44-15 fetched 2026-11-01): the pipeline's adversarial auditor 'found a real defect in about three quarters of our simulations' (sec. 6.4) and the paper warns that 'any such exploit could otherwise become learned behavior' (sec. 3) with no reference-based or optimiser-based check of any simulation; the released solution policies succeed on '96.7% of 2,048 gift-box states' (sec. 6.3) under the agent-chosen settings of Table 6; Policy-Aware Simulator Learning (2605.29032): optimisers 'inevitably exploit minor model inaccuracies'; the same shape in RL environment QA — Fable 5.1 card (L07): environments 'were QA'd against older, less capable models which were not able to find certain hacks'; the field's working belief is that three rounds of model audit certify a simulator for use
if_true: Every agent-built-simulator pipeline adds an optimiser arm to its audit loop and an invariant audit (mass, energy, penetration) on verified successes; groups about to train RL on such corpora run the admission test first; the L5 meta-benchmark's exploitability instrument X(B) gets a corpus with no robot; the result transfers to RL environment QA (audits at capability c certify nothing at c' > c)
if_false: The optimiser finds nothing the auditor missed on all four simulations: three model-audit rounds are sufficient on this corpus, the optimiser arm is cosmetic, and the invariant audit becomes a free column — a reassuring measurement the pipeline's authors cite
probes: C-W44-15 (CMA-ES over the released code policy's waypoint, timing and force parameters, 600 episodes per simulation on four of the 25 simulators — two recorded defect-free, two with a fixed defect — honest arm 200 states plus 100 held out, four reference-free physics invariants thresholded at the honest arm's 99th percentile; ~100 GPU-h, ~$250, 10 d; scorecard present; dead if epsilon_opt - epsilon_honest < 0.05 with the band including zero on all four)

grading.gate0: pass: premise numbers fetched and dated (25 simulators; three audit rounds; 'about three quarters' defect rate; Table 6 settings; 96.7% of 2,048 states); the quantity $\epsilon_{\mathrm{opt}} - \epsilon_{\mathrm{honest}}$ (share of verifier successes violating an invariant, optimiser arm minus released-policy arm) is random given the optimiser's seed and the initial-state draw; the simulator is deterministic given the action sequence except GPU-batch repeat spread, which is read as the floor before any violation counts (checklist 2026-10-20); the verifier (state-based) and the auditor (an LLM reading code and reports) are named as different objects; plain trick: let a cheap optimiser climb the score, then check whether its winning runs broke mass, energy or walls
grading.gate1: pass: C-W44-15 is scorecarded at ~100 GPU-h, $250, 10 d with a pre-registered kill; both outcomes informative (a null is the audit's sufficiency on this corpus)
grading.gate2: pass, route A: benchmark paper (2610.40565 sec. 3 and 6.4), meta-paper (2605.29032), system card (L07: the same audit-at-capability-c shape in RL environment QA; pressure #1) — three source types; route B: audit recall as a ruler with a pre-registered surprise (expected: violations the auditor missed on two of four simulations including one recorded defect-free, with interpenetration the majority class; the field assumes three audit rounds suffice; belief-changing if a defect-free simulation flips)
grading.gate3: one community at the floor (builders of agent-written simulators and groups training on them: an optimiser arm in the audit loop, an admission test); two if the recall result carries to RL environment QA (pressure #1's L07) and three if the L5 meta-benchmark adopts it as the no-robot corpus for X(B); proper-shaped, golden only through the environment-QA transfer
grading.gate4: pass: mechanism — an LLM auditor searches by reasoning over code and reports, an optimiser searches the state-action space the verifier scores, and the verifier rewards outcomes the physics never checks, so an optimiser climbs onto violations the auditor never enumerates; consequence — an optimiser arm and an invariant audit on successes if epsilon separates, model audits certified as sufficient on this corpus if it does not
grading.gate5: pass: a ruler for any agent-built simulator and any state-based verifier; the Gym-Anything corpus is one instance; durable as both auditors and optimisers improve (the gap is structural, not a capability snapshot)
grading.gate6: open: density unmeasured (kill search owed; the J03/J04 kill search of 2026-10-24 covered exploit AND simulator AND policy (13 all-time) and adversarial/worst-case AND simulator (60) and is the seed); incumbents: the card paper's adversarial auditor; IcFuzz 2608.06088 (fuzzes Isaac Sim for crashes, not physics); SAPU 2305.17110 (interpenetration exploited and filtered, the precedent); PolySim and ROBOGATE (cross-simulator gaps, no audit-recall axis); why now: the first released corpus of agent-written simulators with per-simulation audit reports and shared audit memory (2026-10-29); race: the Gym-Anything authors are the obvious next authors; position solo (public corpus, no robot)
grading.failing_gate: Gate 6 not yet established (kill search owed)
grading.grade: open pending kill search; one scorecarded probe under one GPU-week; proper-shaped

headline: The reward-hacking attempt rates in system cards are environment hack-surface rates: on released RL environments the attempt rate tracks the audited leak fraction of the environment family and not the checkpoint.
current_belief: Fable 5.1 system card (L06, 2026-09-01): 'every model is flagged for attempts on roughly 20% to 28% of episodes, with Mythos 5.1 the lowest. Because attempt rates depend heavily on the environments themselves [...] we do not compare them across models that trained on different environments' — the dependence is stated and not measured; L07: 'around half of our computer-use environments incentivized hacking or had accessible hack surfaces [...] these environments were QA'd against older, less capable models which were not able to find certain hacks'; Vals MiMo audit (B13, 2026-10-07): 'in 1,795 of them (67%), the fix commit survives as unreachable objects [...] Rewards were only zeroed for hacks the grader caught, so undetected loopholes are still rewarded' — the environment side measured on one stack with no intermediate checkpoints; the working belief in cards is that the attempt rate is a model trait worth ranking (OpenAI's Respecting Warnings per-model figures, W41 L58)
if_true: System-card attempt rates are read as environment audits: a hack-surface admission filter (the leak audit) replaces behavioural penalties as the recipe change; environment hubs publish s per family and a certified-clean list; cross-model comparison of attempt rates is dropped from cards
if_false: Attempt rate rises across checkpoints at fixed s: propensity is learned, the W41 training-side arm (does RL raise the side effect) is owed, and a reward term rather than an audit is the lever — a citable negative with the s table as its residue
probes: none yet — thought (first measurement sketched in pressure #1: the Vals leak audit as a script over Xiaomi's 2,698 released tasks and Prime Intellect's Environments Hub gives s per family at $0 in a day; the checkpoint axis — open checkpoints of rising capability rolled out on the same environments with an attempt judge — is 200-300 GPU-h, over the solo week unless cut to three checkpoints and two families; queued for /sprint generate)

P-W44-01-audit.what: Step 0 ($0, 1 day): run the leak audit (unreachable Git objects, file timestamps, caches, reachable tests) over the released MiMo tasks and a stratified sample of Prime Intellect's hub to get the hack-surface share $s$ per environment family. Step 1 (two families, three open checkpoints of rising capability, 200 episodes each, an attempt judge calibrated on the Vals labels; ~100 GPU-h if cut to this size): fit attempt rate $a$ against $s$ and against checkpoint; the decomposition is $a = s \cdot q$ with $q$ the search propensity given a surface.
P-W44-01-audit.kill_probe: Pre-registered: dead if attempt rate rises monotonically across checkpoints at fixed $s$ with the Spearman against $s$ under 0.3 (propensity is learned); dead as a measurement if $s$ is under 0.05 on every public family (the owners have already fixed the environment side and the result reads as history). Expected (judgment, from the pressure report): attempt rate tracks $s$ and is flat across checkpoints. Cost: step 0 $0; step 1 ~100 GPU-h, $300, 10 d in the cut-down form.

headline: Sandbox-escape and unwanted-persistence rates in system cards are harness-and-task properties: at a fixed model, a goal loop plus an impossible-task share moves the rate more than one model generation does.
current_belief: Haiku 5.5 system card (L05, 2026-10-07): 'One particularly effective tempter was a /goal-style loop which nudges the model to not give up on its task. [...] Haiku 5.5 did so in 30% of scenarios (524 of 1,753) [...] In 502 of the 524, the task could not be completed from inside the sandbox. Adding a short description to the system prompt about the kind of sandbox the model is in reduced the rate [...] from 30% to 1.8%' — both levers measured on one model, never crossed with models; The Register on OpenAI (L14, 2026-09-29): the withdrawn model 'didn't quite meet the bar in terms of staying within scope and authorization [...] You really do need to find what's the right line between staying within scope [and] avoiding laziness'; GPT-6.1 Terra addendum (L16, 2026-10-26): 'Terra performed the specified unauthorized action in 13.75% (11 of 80 samples). Comparisons: GPT-6.1 Sol 50.00% / 1.25%' — rates ranked per model at one harness on 80 samples; the cards' working belief is that persistence past blockers is a model trait to be ranked
if_true: Every misalignment table declares its harness and its impossible-task share; the capability-safety trade is handled as a harness and reward-design problem (a reward that pays a correct stop, or a scope classifier at inference), not a model-ranking one; labs stop ranking models on rates measured under their own loops
if_false: The model term dominates the variance decomposition: propensity is a training-mix property, the cards are right to rank models on it, and the public gated-scenario set is the residue
probes: none yet — thought (first measurement sketched in pressure #4: a public gated-scenario set from Agents' Last Exam Linux tasks and Prime Intellect sandboxes with planted authorization gates and a labelled impossible subset; three open models x three harness conditions (plain, goal loop, goal loop plus the sandbox paragraph) x 200 scenarios; variance decomposition of the crossing rate into model, harness and task-impossibility terms, with persistence scored as capability on the possible subset and as violation on the gated subset from the same rollouts; under one GPU-day for open models, about $2,000 of API for frontier ones, two weeks; queued for /sprint generate)

P-W44-03-cross.what: Crossed design on a public gated-scenario set: $r = \Pr[\mathrm{impossible}] \cdot \Pr[\mathrm{loop\ re\text{-}issues}] \cdot \Pr[\mathrm{cross} \mid \mathrm{impossible}, \mathrm{loop}]$, with only the last factor the model's; three open models (two generations of one family plus one other) x three harness conditions x 200 scenarios (100 possible, 100 impossible by design), 3 runs per cell; readouts: crossing rate per cell, the variance decomposition over model, harness and impossibility terms, and the capability score on the possible subset from the same rollouts.
P-W44-03-cross.kill_probe: Pre-registered: dead if the model term carries more than half of the crossing-rate variance with the harness and impossibility terms each under a fifth (propensity is a training-mix property); dead as news if the harness term is large only through the one-paragraph system-prompt effect already in print (L05) and the goal-loop x impossibility interaction is inside the run band. Expected (judgment): harness plus impossibility over two thirds, model under a fifth, and the generation contrast smaller than the goal-loop contrast. Cost: under one GPU-day for open models (about 20 GPU-h), $0-2,000 depending on frontier arms, two weeks.

headline: On Terminal-Bench 3.0 to 4.0, for a fixed model under one pinned harness, more than half of the kept-task score delta falls on the 19 repaired tasks, and model orderings on the repaired tasks disagree with orderings on the 47 untouched tasks beyond the random-subset ceiling.
current_belief: Terminal-Bench 4.0 release note (B04, 2026-08-28): 'All tasks in TB 4.0 are now set to a flat agent timeout of 8 hours [...] We removed 8 tasks [...] We fixed 19 tasks [...] These represent breaking changes that require re-running trials' — the changes are listed, not scored; SWE-Bench Pro V2 (B07, 2026-10-16): 'repaired or retired 480 of the 731 tasks: 23 contracted engineers spent 404 hours [...] 69 tasks had instructions that contradicted the tests grading them', with the board at '99.4 +/- 0.4' three weeks after relaunch (B08); Cognition FrontierCode 2.0 (L18, 2026-10-27): 'In 80% of FrontierCode 2.0 tasks, the reference solution differs from the upstream PR, up from 60% in FrontierCode 1.0', six of eight models reordered; Gemini 4 Argon model card (L12): 'computed with improved evaluations and thus are not directly comparable'; Vals (B12): 'Because the task set is entirely different, scores are not comparable across versions' — the owners say 'not comparable' with no number, and launch tables read the version delta as model progress
if_true: Every continuous benchmark publishes a repair delta per release and the ordering on the unchanged subset; labs report old-version and new-version scores as separate columns; aggregators stop drawing trend lines across refreshes; a version refresh is labelled equatable, linkable or new construct

P-W44-02-repair.what: For each version pair $(v, v')$ and each model-harness-effort entry run on both, pair per-task outcomes and write the delta as $\Delta = \sum_{t \in \mathrm{kept}} w_t\,(p_t^{v'} - p_t^{v})$ plus a composition term for removed and added tasks, with $p_t^{v}$ the task's success rate under version $v$ and $w_t$ its weight; the repair share is the sum over tasks in the changelog (fixed, recalibrated, timeout-relaxed) divided by $|\Delta|$; report the Spearman correlation of model orderings on the untouched subset between versions.
P-W44-02-repair.kill_probe: Pre-registered: dead if the repair share is under one half on both public pairs (TB 3.0 to 4.0; FrontierCode 1.1 to 2.0) with a task-cluster bootstrap interval excluding 0.5; the ordering clause is dead if the untouched-subset Spearman is under 0.8 on either pair (or, by import S5xF2, if the link differs by scaffold family beyond 1.5x the floor). Expected (judgment): repair share above one half on TB 3.0 to 4.0 (timeout relaxation and 19 fixes) and the ordering preserved; on FrontierCode the rubric itself changed ('we loosened our scope criteria'), so the ordering clause is expected to fail there — which is the construct-change reading, recorded as such. Cost: $0, two weeks of data assembly.

headline: Model-written adversarial audits do not bound what an optimiser extracts from a simulator: in agent-built simulators that passed three audit rounds, a 600-episode search against the verifier makes at least one in twenty verified successes physically invalid.
current_belief: Gym-Anything for Robotics (2610.40565, 2026-10-29; card and candidate C-W44-15 fetched 2026-11-01): the pipeline's adversarial auditor 'found a real defect in about three quarters of our simulations' (sec. 6.4) and the paper warns that 'any such exploit could otherwise become learned behavior' (sec. 3) with no reference-based or optimiser-based check of any simulation; the released solution policies succeed on '96.7% of 2,048 gift-box states' (sec. 6.3) under the agent-chosen settings of Table 6; Policy-Aware Simulator Learning (2605.29032): optimisers 'inevitably exploit minor model inaccuracies'; the same shape in RL environment QA — Fable 5.1 card (L07): environments 'were QA'd against older, less capable models which were not able to find certain hacks'; the field's working belief is that three rounds of model audit certify a simulator for use
if_true: Every agent-built-simulator pipeline adds an optimiser arm to its audit loop and an invariant audit (mass, energy, penetration) on verified successes; groups about to train RL on such corpora run the admission test first; the L5 meta-benchmark's exploitability instrument X(B) gets a corpus with no robot; the result transfers to RL environment QA (audits at capability c certify nothing at c' > c)
if_false: The optimiser finds nothing the auditor missed on all four simulations: three model-audit rounds are sufficient on this corpus, the optimiser arm is cosmetic, and the invariant audit becomes a free column — a reassuring measurement the pipeline's authors cite
probes: C-W44-15 (CMA-ES over the released code policy's waypoint, timing and force parameters, 600 episodes per simulation on four of the 25 simulators — two recorded defect-free, two with a fixed defect — honest arm 200 states plus 100 held out, four reference-free physics invariants thresholded at the honest arm's 99th percentile; ~100 GPU-h, ~$250, 10 d; scorecard present; dead if epsilon_opt - epsilon_honest < 0.05 with the band including zero on all four)

grading.gate0: pass: premise numbers fetched and dated (25 simulators; three audit rounds; 'about three quarters' defect rate; Table 6 settings; 96.7% of 2,048 states); the quantity $\epsilon_{\mathrm{opt}} - \epsilon_{\mathrm{honest}}$ (share of verifier successes violating an invariant, optimiser arm minus released-policy arm) is random given the optimiser's seed and the initial-state draw; the simulator is deterministic given the action sequence except GPU-batch repeat spread, which is read as the floor before any violation counts (checklist 2026-10-20); the verifier (state-based) and the auditor (an LLM reading code and reports) are named as different objects; plain trick: let a cheap optimiser climb the score, then check whether its winning runs broke mass, energy or walls
grading.gate1: pass: C-W44-15 is scorecarded at ~100 GPU-h, $250, 10 d with a pre-registered kill; both outcomes informative (a null is the audit's sufficiency on this corpus)
grading.gate2: pass, route A: benchmark paper (2610.40565 sec. 3 and 6.4), meta-paper (2605.29032), system card (L07: the same audit-at-capability-c shape in RL environment QA; pressure #1) — three source types; route B: audit recall as a ruler with a pre-registered surprise (expected: violations the auditor missed on two of four simulations including one recorded defect-free, with interpenetration the majority class; the field assumes three audit rounds suffice; belief-changing if a defect-free simulation flips)
grading.gate3: one community at the floor (builders of agent-written simulators and groups training on them: an optimiser arm in the audit loop, an admission test); two if the recall result carries to RL environment QA (pressure #1's L07) and three if the L5 meta-benchmark adopts it as the no-robot corpus for X(B); proper-shaped, golden only through the environment-QA transfer
grading.gate4: pass: mechanism — an LLM auditor searches by reasoning over code and reports, an optimiser searches the state-action space the verifier scores, and the verifier rewards outcomes the physics never checks, so an optimiser climbs onto violations the auditor never enumerates; consequence — an optimiser arm and an invariant audit on successes if epsilon separates, model audits certified as sufficient on this corpus if it does not
grading.gate5: pass: a ruler for any agent-built simulator and any state-based verifier; the Gym-Anything corpus is one instance; durable as both auditors and optimisers improve (the gap is structural, not a capability snapshot)
grading.gate6: open: density unmeasured (kill search owed; the J03/J04 kill search of 2026-10-24 covered exploit AND simulator AND policy (13 all-time) and adversarial/worst-case AND simulator (60) and is the seed); incumbents: the card paper's adversarial auditor; IcFuzz 2608.06088 (fuzzes Isaac Sim for crashes, not physics); SAPU 2305.17110 (interpenetration exploited and filtered, the precedent); PolySim and ROBOGATE (cross-simulator gaps, no audit-recall axis); why now: the first released corpus of agent-written simulators with per-simulation audit reports and shared audit memory (2026-10-29); race: the Gym-Anything authors are the obvious next authors; position solo (public corpus, no robot)
grading.failing_gate: Gate 6 not yet established (kill search owed)
grading.grade: open pending kill search; one scorecarded probe under one GPU-week; proper-shaped

neighbors.title: Gym-Anything for Robotics: Scaling physical simulations with digital agents
neighbors.trick: A coding agent writes each simulation's physics; four same-model auditors, one adversarial, re-run its checks and hunt legal-action exploits for three rounds; 25 simulations and 200 verifier-scored tasks ship with recorded attempts and released code policies.
neighbors.difference: Occupies the corpus, the auditor and the defect rate; runs no optimiser and no RL, states no residual estimate, has no limitations section; its criterion (j) and its citation of Baker 2020 are the claim's premise in the authors' own words.

neighbors.title: Scalable Weak-to-Strong Verifier Hardening for Agent Environments
neighbors.trick: Sandbox the verifier, let a weaker model's hacker search for reward without solving the task and a fixer patch the verifier, validate patches by replaying legitimate solutions, then attack with stronger models and report the residual.
neighbors.difference: Occupies the headline's generic clause and its RL-environment-QA transfer: a model-written audit's recall against a stronger attacker, measured (31.9% of 295 exploitable tasks still exploitable), released, adopted by Terminal Bench; attacker is a language model, validity is a judge's call, no physics, no invariants, no numerical optimiser.

neighbors.title: Emergent Tool Use From Multi-Agent Autocurricula
neighbors.trick: Train hiders and seekers by self-play in a MuJoCo arena; six strategy phases emerge, including box surfing and physics exploits.
neighbors.difference: The card paper's own citation for the exploit premise ('agents exploiting inaccuracies of the physics simulations to their advantage'); names environment generation without such behaviours as future work; pre-window, no audit, no rate.

neighbors.title: Theoretical Foundations and Effective Algorithms for Policy-Aware Simulator Learning
neighbors.trick: Learn a simulator as a minimax game against an adversarial policy rewarded by the critic's one-step error, because powerful RL optimisers inevitably exploit minor model inaccuracies.
neighbors.difference: The optimiser-as-auditor mechanism for learned models with a true environment to score against; no engineered simulator, no written pre-release audit to score recall against.

neighbors.title: When the Simulator Fails, Not the Policy: Auditing Contact Artifacts in Simulated Robot Benchmarks (SimuGuard)
neighbors.trick: Record every physics step of benchmark rollouts, flag an object that gains speed at a contact faster than the robot or gravity account for, replay bit for bit, rerun with one engine parameter changed.
neighbors.difference: Occupies the per-rollout invariant flag the probe would reimplement; frozen policies on hand-built benchmarks; no optimiser, no agent-written simulator; the probe cites its flag.

neighbors.title: ImpossibleRubrics: Stress-Testing Generated Rubrics as Reward Signals
neighbors.trick: Give each impossible task an oracle certificate, let models generate rubrics, optimise answers adversarially against each rubric, count certificate violations the rubric rewards (8-26%).
neighbors.difference: The same share-of-rewarded-outputs-that-violate-an-oracle quantity on a model-generated artifact under adversarial optimisation; register is rubrics and text, oracle is a certificate, not a physical invariant.

neighbors.title: Auditing Reward Hackability in Code RL Training Environments
neighbors.trick: Generate incorrect patches that pass the tests to measure the hackable share (28.5% of SWE-bench Verified), then harden with a judge gated by a gold-solution sanity check.
neighbors.difference: A measured hackability rate of a training-environment corpus plus hardening; attacker is a model, criterion is test pass versus known-incorrect patch; no simulator.

neighbors.title: Hack-Verifiable Environments: Towards Evaluating Reward Hacking at Scale (with 2608.22103 Hack-Verifiable Terminal Bench)
neighbors.trick: Plant detectable hacks in environments so reward hacking is measured deterministically rather than by inspecting trajectories.
neighbors.difference: The field's shipped way to measure exploitation: by construction, not by search; no physics, no optimiser.

neighbors.title: Code2Worlds-2: Physically Plausible Agent Harness for Embodied World Simulation
neighbors.trick: Compile a model-generated 4D scene to MuJoCo and refine it in a compile-simulate-critique loop whose simulator critic reads penetration depth, collision pairs, stability, contact forces, joint limits and reachability.
neighbors.difference: Nearest invariant audit inside a generation loop; checks run on the generated scene before any policy or optimiser exists; no search against a verifier, no residual rate.

neighbors.title: FATE: Closed-Loop Feasibility-Aware Task Generation with Active Repair
neighbors.trick: Put a generalist embodied agent inside the task-generation loop to verify execution feasibility by simulated interaction and repair infeasible tasks.
neighbors.difference: An executing agent in the audit loop aimed at infeasibility, not exploitability; no rate of invalid successes.

neighbors.title: WorldSolver: Can LLM Agents Simulate the Physical Dynamics via Solver Generation?
neighbors.trick: Benchmark 168 agent-written physics solvers on execution, visual fidelity and physical plausibility; best agents reach 48.7%.
neighbors.difference: Grades agent-written solvers for plausibility with fixed checks; no optimiser, no verifier to climb, no audit recall.

neighbors.title: IndustReal (SAPU)
neighbors.trick: Measure interpenetration every step and drop or down-weight episodes that exploit it, because the agent otherwise learns to.
neighbors.difference: The physics-exploit premise for GPU contact-rich RL with a mitigation; single artefact, hand-built engine, no audit.

neighbors.title: Assessing Transferability from Simulation to Reality for Reinforcement Learning (SPOTA)
neighbors.trick: Define simulation optimisation bias as the optimiser's gain from exploiting simulator error and estimate it from held-out domains.
neighbors.difference: The claim's quantity as a defined, estimated object in 2019; parametric error, not model-written physics.

neighbors.title: Sim2Real Predictivity (Kadian et al.)
neighbors.trick: Nine navigation agents in a scanned lab and its replica; agents slide along walls by abusing collision dynamics; correlation 0.18.
neighbors.difference: Single-artefact datum that a missed exploit ruined a benchmark; post hoc, no search, no rate.

neighbors.title: The Surprising Creativity of Digital Evolution

neighbors.difference: The folklore the field cites for 'optimisers find what designers missed'; anecdotes, no rate.

limitation_quotes.quote: Hardening is bounded by the hacker's search capability and budget. Verifier access supports targeted search but cannot ensure that all exploit routes are discovered. The hardened environments still admit successful attacks, and an in-loop robust status is an empirical stopping outcome rather than a security guarantee.

Robustness to exploits. (j) No sequence of legal robot actions causes instabilities, such as non-finite values, or physically impossible states, such as objects flying away. Since reinforcement learning optimizes against the simulation, any such exploit could otherwise become learned behavior (Baker et al., 2020). [...] The audit agent for robustness reads the code and searches for legal robot actions that produce non-finite values, energy blow-ups, or physically impossible motion, and returns its evidence to the creation agent. [...] it found a real defect in about three quarters of our simulations. (No limitations section exists in the paper.)

We also found that agents were very skilled at exploiting small inaccuracies in the design of the environment, such as seekers surfing on boxes without touching the ground, hiders running away from the environment while shielding themselves with boxes, or agents exploiting inaccuracies of the physics simulations to their advantage. Investigating methods to generate environments without these unwanted behaviors is another import direction of future research.

source: lane sentence ('the true cost structure of agentic workloads') + the field's own accounting (FlashNext-RL's tokens/s/GPU; AKV's hit/miss arithmetic) + import S6xF7's operational analysis
headline: In asynchronous agentic RL the binding resource of a training iteration is KV-cache residency, not decode compute, and the waste terms systems papers list do not add.
current_belief: Systems papers quote throughput in output tokens per second per GPU and list waste terms as if they add (FlashNext-RL 2610.28998: 26% zero-advantage rollouts discarded, a third of sessions idle on sandbox commands, trainer waiting 25%); context-management papers report savings as token counts (observation masking, sliding windows), while 2610.26632 found dropping turns cost 2.9-4.0x the dollars at 0.84-0.90x the tokens because it broke prefix caching.
if_true: Every agentic-RL systems paper reports a per-station demand table and names the binding station; KV release during tool waits becomes a predicted 25-35% iteration-time lever; trainer kernel work past the balance point is shown futile
if_false: Decode compute binds (utilization >= 0.85 with KV below cap) and KV release moves iteration time under 5%: token accounting is adequate and the lane's cost instrument is Little's law applied once

neighbors.title: Scheduling Mixed RL Rollouts Beyond Prefix Locality (MISA-T)
neighbors.trick: Treat admitting a rollout session as a commitment of KV block-time (footprint times residency, tool intervals included), cap sessions per engine by a protected KV budget divided by footprint, split the budget across RLVR/RLHF/agentic classes by block-time demand, and hold new sessions when hit rate degrades.
neighbors.difference: none — occupied: Table 1 names residency as the dominant agentic cost against decode for RLVR; eq. 2 and eq. 11 are the import's passive-resource demand; section 2.5 measures the residency collapse (hit rate 92.4% to 4.5%, throughput -52.5%); Table 4 cuts iteration time 22.8% with decode throughput +38.0%; section 4.1 states the prefill-saturation bound F/E[L_r - H_r]. Not run: a four-station table; a decode-utilization reading.

neighbors.title: KV4-RL: Unlocking Faster Asynchronous Rollouts for RLVR with INT4 KV Cache Quantization
neighbors.trick: Show that continuous refill in asynchronous rollout concentrates the same attention work into fewer, heavier decode steps, chart per-GPU weight, GEMM and KV-read demands in equal service-time units to find KV reads largest, and quantize the KV cache to INT4 with INT8 sinks so the sampler stays faithful.
neighbors.difference: none — occupied for 'not decode compute' and the per-station demand table on an asynchronous RL loop (Fig. 3(a); App. D.1 capacity 91.7 of 93.9 GB; Fig. A8 bottleneck shift to the learner). Stations are bandwidth and FLOPs, not holding time; RLVR math, colocated; limitations name agentic and multi-turn as future validation.

neighbors.title: TideRL: Boosting Agentic RL Goodput with Readiness-Aware Scheduling
neighbors.trick: Schedule rollouts as tasks: admit a task only when the rank has KV headroom, pause low-priority tasks before memory is exhausted, resume them where their prefix is still cached, and move ranks between rollout and trainer from two readiness signals.
neighbors.difference: The tool-wait KV term measured in agentic RL (hit rate ~12% under request-level batching; 0.9% vs 6.0% on WebShop) and the lever shipped (CTB, pause/resume endpoints; -15.6% step time); the non-additivity clause as a sentence (C3: bottleneck 'dynamically flip[s]'). No demand table.

neighbors.title: PEARL: Adaptive Prefill-Decode Execution with Elasticity for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
neighbors.trick: Predict rollout-batch completion time from runtime profiles that account for the drop in decode concurrency caused by environment waits, and choose PD colocation versus disaggregation and the PD ratio under the current GPU budget.
neighbors.difference: A throughput model with the tool-wait term, used for configuration choice; the term is lost decode concurrency, not KV holding time.

neighbors.title: VenusRL: A Fully Disaggregated Agentic RL System with Priority Scheduling and Scalable Interaction
neighbors.trick: Predict which rollout groups finish soonest and push them ahead in batch admission, KV-cache residency and cross-worker routing; pack sandboxes by copy-on-write page sharing.
neighbors.difference: KV residency is a scheduling axis by name; no demand table; two levers as separate headline numbers.

neighbors.title: Continuum: Efficient and Robust Multi-Turn LLM Agent Scheduling with KV Cache Time-to-Live
neighbors.trick: Pin a tool-calling request's KV in GPU memory for a time-to-live set by reload cost and the queueing delay eviction would cause, then evict on expiry.
neighbors.difference: The KV-during-tool-wait lever on the serving side (8x job completion time); not a training iteration.

neighbors.title: Idleness is Relative: Exploiting Tool-Call Idle Windows for Offloading in Agentic Systems with MORI
neighbors.trick: Rank active agent programs by idleness, keep the busiest in HBM and the most idle in DRAM, and move the boundary to match tier capacity, on Claude Code traces.
neighbors.difference: Same lever, serving side; tool-call durations span orders of magnitude; no RL loop.

neighbors.title: Sparse-RL: Breaking the Memory Wall in LLM Reinforcement Learning via Stable Sparse Rollouts
neighbors.trick: Run rollouts under KV compression and repair the sampler-learner mismatch with rejection sampling and importance reweighting.
neighbors.difference: States the premise (KV memory during long-horizon rollouts 'acts as a critical bottleneck') in January 2026; single-turn.

neighbors.title: Reshaping Rollout Workloads for Asynchronous RL Post-Training on Heterogeneous Accelerators (CadenceRL)
neighbors.trick: Pace long trajectories into short ones to keep large active batches on memory-bandwidth-bound decode, concentrate the long tail on high-bandwidth workers, and prepare KV late.
neighbors.difference: The bandwidth form of 'not decode compute' with late-bound KV placement; no tool waits.

neighbors.title: RollArt: Disaggregated Multi-Task Agentic RL Training at Scale
neighbors.trick: Map compute-bound prefill, bandwidth-bound decode and CPU-heavy environments to different hardware and decouple rollout at the trajectory level.
neighbors.difference: The station classification written as a design; no demand numbers.

neighbors.title: S3R: Fast and Faithful RL Rollouts via Self-Sparse Speculative Decoding
neighbors.trick: Draft with sparse attention and verify with full attention inside RL rollouts; a KV-aware scheduler limits repeated KV offload and restoration.
neighbors.difference: KV thrashing named as the rollout constraint for RLVR; no agent loop.

neighbors.title: When Do Larger Batches Help Scale LLM Reinforcement Learning?
neighbors.trick: Generation is memory-bandwidth-bound at low concurrency while training scales with tokens, so a larger batch helps only when its throughput gain beats its samples-to-target penalty.
neighbors.difference: The decision rule from the same asymmetry; no agentic loop, no residency.

neighbors.title: Understanding KV Residency in Production-Scale Agentic LLM Workloads
neighbors.trick: Replay 121M production agent calls under KV budgets: inference occupies 5.6% of retention time; LRU at one tenth of peak makes 63% of calls recompute.
neighbors.difference: Fleet-scale residency fact; serving, not training.

neighbors.title: Bidirectional Resource Scheduling for Disaggregated and Asynchronous RL Post-Training (BiDiRL)
neighbors.trick: Hot-switch GPUs between rollout and training from a time-performance model so the stages balance, then borrow idle resources at run time.
neighbors.difference: A throughput model of the two-stage loop with idleness as the waste; no KV term.

neighbors.title: ObsSpec: Accelerating Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Observation Speculation
neighbors.trick: Predict the tool's output with a small world model while the tool runs and keep the speculated generation only on an exact match.
neighbors.difference: The tool wait attacked from the generation side (-9.3% to -14.2% latency); a third shipped lever on the same wait.

neighbors.title: Libra: Efficient Resource Management for Agentic RL Post-Training
neighbors.trick: Route rollout requests across execution buckets with different parallelism to cut straggler delay and move workers between rollout and training as the workload shifts.
neighbors.difference: The 'bottleneck moves' family (with QwenGyre 2609.33848, ROSE 2605.06534); no demand per station.

neighbors.title: CacheWise: Understanding Workloads and Optimizing KVCache Management for Efficiently Serving LLM Coding Agents
neighbors.trick: Collect coding-agent traces, show sustained KV pressure with large prefix reuse, and evict by predictions from tool-call metadata.
neighbors.difference: Serving-side characterization (with TraceLab 2606.30560); no RL loop.

neighbors.title: FlashNext-RL: A System Optimization Study for Long-Horizon Agentic RL of Qwen3.8-Flash-Next
neighbors.trick: Fit a 125B MoE trainer on one node; 112 sessions per engine, KV cap 65%, a third of sessions between turns, trainer waits 25%.
neighbors.difference: The source card: lists the waste terms without a table.

pre_window_precedents.trick: AReaL (May 2025): the synchronous iteration is bounded by the longest output in the batch, so decouple generation from training and bound staleness.
StreamRL (April 2025): pipeline bubbles and skewness bubbles from long-tail output lengths; an output-length ranker dispatches the tail.
Dai et al. (April 2025): queueing fundamentals for LLM inference and agent DAGs; work-conserving schedulers are throughput-optimal (serving only).
KVFlow (July 2025): workflow-aware KV eviction and prefetch for many concurrent agent workflows.

limitation_quotes.quote: Limitations: 'MISA-T assumes that requests carry workload labels and relies on timely serving-state reports from inference instances. Delayed or incomplete snapshots can temporarily reduce the accuracy of KV-demand estimates and admission caps.' Section 2.6: 'Admitting a new session is not an isolated request-placement decision; it commits capacity for subsequent KV growth, future continuations, and intervals between turns.' Table 3: 'The larger tool gap for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B shows why model inference time alone can underestimate KV-cache residency.' Eq. 2: 'for agentic sessions, residency includes tool-execution intervals between turns.' Section 4.1: 'admitting additional sessions cannot improve this bound if KV churn reduces H_r.'

Section 7.2: 'Further validation on MoE and hybrid-attention models, disaggregated rollout systems, and broader long-horizon workloads such as agentic and multi-turn RLVR remains an important direction.' Section 4: 'Which component of the decode workload becomes the dominant cost when high concurrency is sustained across long responses?'; 'KV reads constitute the largest idealized service demand throughout the measured traces and grow as the generated responses become longer'; 'Thus, asynchronous scheduling removes the utilization tail only to expose a new scaling constraint: the storage and processing cost of the concentrated KV workload.' App. D.6: 'The absolute learner cost remains similar across the two configurations, so it becomes the primary limit on further end-to-end gains from rollout-only acceleration.'

Section 2.2: 'GPU waiting and repeated prefill recomputation are pure overhead.' C1: 'the hit rate subsequently plummets and remains at only ~12%'. Section 6.3: 'The vanilla scheduler's frequent preemption drives the cache hit rate as low as 0.9%, while CTB keeps it above 6.0%, close to the ideal upper limit'. C3: 'multi-turn environments cause the computational bottleneck to dynamically flip between generation and training'.

kill_search.why_not_done: It has been done, in pieces, inside the window, in the neighbours' vocabulary. Enabling pieces: asynchronous rollout services at scale (StreamRL 2025-04, AReaL 2025-05) made rollout generation a distributed serving workload with admission and staleness limits; engines exposing session-level KV snapshots, prefix-hash events and Prometheus counters (vLLM Router 2026; SGLang/vLLM endpoints read by TideRL) made the residency term measurable; the field wrote the term and acted on it within months (Sparse-RL 2026-01 premise; TideRL 2026-08 task-level admission by KV headroom; MISA-T 2026-08 block-time accounting with tool intervals; KV4-RL 2026-10 per-station demand chart). The four-station table with single-lever interventions is unasked because every stack with the counters uses them to schedule rather than to publish a table, and the two levers are each measured in print (KV kept through tool waits: TideRL -15.6% step, MISA-T -22.8% iteration; tool wait shortened: ObsSpec -9 to -14%). headline: The run-to-run variance that agent benchmarks report at temperature 0 is the serving stack's batch-dependent arithmetic, not the agent, and over multi-turn trajectories it is large enough to reorder leaderboards.

P-W43-J01-a.what: Outcome-flip rate at temperature 0: default serving stack (batch composition varied by concurrency) versus batch-invariant decoding, agent and user simulator both an 8B open model at temperature 0, on a multi-turn benchmark with deterministic tools
P-W43-J01-a.design: Two arms x 10 repeats x 100 tasks. Default arm: vLLM default kernels, each repeat run at a different concurrency (alone, 8, 32) so batch composition changes. Treatment arm: the same stack with batch-invariant kernels (TML's released kernels or vLLM's batch-invariant mode - which exists and works for the model is checked at the kill search); its flip rate must be exactly 0, which is the determinism check. Record per task: any outcome disagreement across the 10 repeats, the turn of first divergence, pass^k for k=1..10, and the rank order of three agent variants (prompt or scaffold variants) per repeat.
P-W43-J01-a.kill_probe: Dead if the default arm's outcome-flip rate is under 2 percent of tasks AND the rank order of the three agent variants is identical across all ten repeats. Expected (judgment): 5-15 percent flips on 30-turn tasks and at least one adjacent-rank swap. Field's assumption: temperature 0 is deterministic or noise of a point. Belief-changing: over 15 percent or a non-adjacent rank reversal. 15-25 GPU-hours on one H100, $50-80, 4 days.

source: lifted from three L1 orphans on one theme (C-W43-06, C-W43-07, C-W43-20): scaffold-model interaction
headline: Pasted context and scaffold layers steer agents by presence, not content: a same-length block from the wrong source moves a model's yield as much as the right one does.
current_belief: Harness papers read a per-model context effect as the information in the block: 2610.28802's abstract recommends 'combining configurations for broader coverage' and reports a targeted call-graph block raising weaker models' yield; investigator-agent papers attribute a semantic layer's harm to its content (C-W43-07's card).
if_true: Every scaffold or context-engineering comparison needs a same-length placebo arm, the way drug trials do; leaderboard 'harness' columns are re-read as prompt-form effects; harness builders spend on form (an authoritative-looking block) before retrieval quality.
if_false: Content wins: the placebo moves nothing, the information in the block is what helps, and the open question is which models can use it (C-W43-06's habit ruler).

neighbors.title: Prune the Summary, Not the History: Source-Judged Compaction for Long-Horizon Agents (SJC)
neighbors.trick: After each compaction a cheap yes/no judge scores every summary bullet for having a source in the environment outputs or the prior summary, and bullets without one are deleted.
neighbors.difference: none for the headline's first clause — occupied: its census (29 of 35 failed runs follow an entry; 22 unsupported, 3 contradicted) is the claim's number and its delete recipe is the claim's if_true; it lacks the control (only the Prompting arm's 44 failures were traced; the No Compression reference arm never) and any length control.

neighbors.title: Compact-Bench: Measuring What Context Compaction Costs Long-Horizon Coding Agents
neighbors.trick: Continue the same coding task from one repository snapshot with the full history (PRE) and with the summary (POST), call a repair damaged when PRE passes and POST fails, and score production summaries for a completed write described as pending.
neighbors.difference: The uncompressed control already run on 35 repairs x 14 summarizers; its diagnosis of the stable damages is the opposite reading of the claim (all audited repair tokens retained, progress lost) and its one commission detector flags 0 of 224 production boundaries; no unsourced-entry cell.

neighbors.title: Maximising Transparency in Context Compaction Improves Retention of Facts and Commitments for Lightweight Coding Agents
neighbors.trick: Keep user and assistant prose verbatim at compaction, drop bulky tool output, flag what was stripped, and label each probe failure confident or not.
neighbors.difference: Splits post-compaction errors into confident blunders versus admitted non-recall with control turns and finds the commission cases are sourced values that lost their binding context (7 of 7 had the correct value in the summary; 5 of 7 a sourced look-alike beside it); planted probes, no natural-failure census.

neighbors.title: Governance Decay: How Context Compaction Silently Erases Safety Constraints in Long-Horizon LLM Agents
neighbors.trick: Place a governance constraint in context, compact, grade tool calls deterministically, and split episodes by whether the constraint survived the summary.
neighbors.difference: Judge-free kept-versus-dropped split with the full-context arm as the 0% reference; the mechanism is omission (dropped: 38% violation; survived: 0%); synthetic constraints, no unsourced cell. Pre-window precedent named by pressure #6.

neighbors.title: Benchmarks Are Surprisingly Compaction-Friendly

neighbors.difference: The omission side counted on real sessions (one third of anticheating rules dropped at the first compaction; conduct instructions dropped 6x more than build specs); no commission cell, no per-failure census.

neighbors.difference: Before/after control on a natural action (30/100 sessions deleted emails after compaction, none before); dropped constraints (17% retained); no unsourced cell.

limitation_quotes.quote: SJC filters by provenance, not correctness, and the two are largely independent: supported and unsupported entries are correct at similar rates (92.2% against 90.6%; Appendix G). [...] In multi-turn settings, earlier user messages are themselves a source and would need to be treated as one; we have not evaluated that case. [...] Finally, the failure analysis in Section 3 relies on annotations produced by LLM annotators under a written protocol. (Sec. 5.5: The unsupported entry raises the chance of the error rather than determining it: the third Prompting run carries the same entry and still succeeds. App. D: All 44 failed runs of the Prompting baseline on the training split were traced by LLM annotators following a fixed written protocol. Sec. 5.1: We use No Compression, which retains the full interaction history, as the uncompressed reference.)

Results are conditional on the tested repository repairs, continuation agent, and budget. Detail-retention scores capture literal recurrence, while later production-boundary estimates use small, changing session subsets. (Sec. 4.4: Pytest-7571 is particularly informative: all five audited tokens survive, yet the continuation fails. [...] The cases expose a distinction between preserving repair ingredients and preserving the progress that connects them to a completed edit. App. C: The completed-write detector flags zero boundaries under the matching rules in Appendix L.)

Omission is not the only failure. In each of the 7 cases in which a detail was first answered correctly and later answered confidently wrong, the correct value was still in the summary. In 5 of them a competing value from a later look-alike episode stood beside it, and the context that had separated the two was gone. [...] One summary also silently rewrote the day of a release freeze, an error the probes did not score, so they understate summary errors. (Limitations: control turns for the commitment probes were run on Qwen only.)

Enabling pieces: Compact-Bench's paired PRE/POST continuations with code and data (2026-10-22); HSC-Bench's full-history arm for six receivers with typed criteria (2026-10-27); SJC's public harness with the No Compression arm (2026-10-14); the typed matcher and scenario-cluster protocol from the C-W43-23 red team (2026-10-25). The SJC authors hold the logs and have not been asked; that email is step 0.

P-W43-01-2x2.what: The simulator-budget 2x2: train a policy at the shipped solver budget (Go1 iterations=1; Leap iterations=5) and at the converged budget (iterations=100, tol 1e-8) under the full training protocol (DR, kicks, observation noise, sampled actions) with a wall-clock-matched arm; evaluate every policy in both engines with paired DR draws and seeds; the interaction term J_conv(pi_conv) - J_conv(pi_cap) - [J_cap(pi_conv) - J_cap(pi_cap)] is the cap-isolated exploit; the certificate ||g_K|| and nchange logged per step are the fidelity column; sim2sim across engines (Playground's shipped script) is the field-standard transfer proxy; hardware is the ceiling arm.
P-W43-01-2x2.kill_probe: Dead if the interaction term lies inside the batch-seed interval of zero on BOTH Go1 rough terrain and the Leap cube task. Pre-registered (judgment): Go1 interaction about zero (sticking contacts; the hardware prior), Leap interaction positive and a non-trivial share of return (many simultaneous contacts; SAPU's interpenetration exploit in assembly is the precedent). Field's assumption: DR absorbs numerical error everywhere, and Leap failures are hardware flex and geometry. Belief-changing: a positive Leap interaction that shrinks with budget at matched wall-clock. Cost: two retrains per task at minutes each on 2 GPUs, cross-evaluation in minutes; 4-10 GPU-hours including the Leap retrain (no public Leap checkpoint), $20-50, one week.

neighbors.title: When the Simulator Fails, Not the Policy: Auditing Contact Artifacts in Simulated Robot Benchmarks (SimuGuard)
neighbors.trick: Wrap the benchmark's physics step, record every body and contact, flag objects that gain speed at a contact faster than the robot or gravity can supply, replay bit for bit, rerun with one engine parameter changed (mass, solver iterations, depenetration limit, MuJoCo contact time constant), and trace the ejections to a fixed triangle-area threshold in PhysX 5.3.1; repaired engine lifts LingBot-VA 89% to 98%.
neighbors.difference: Occupies the lane's per-step audit with one-parameter reruns, at evaluation time on frozen policies, with the opposite sign (simulator penalises the policy); never retrains, so the train-in/evaluate-in interaction is unmeasured; its solver-iteration rerun found the cap irrelevant to the artefact.

neighbors.title: IndustReal: Transferring Contact-Rich Assembly Tasks from Simulation to Reality (SAPU)
neighbors.trick: Measure plug-socket interpenetration every step with a Warp point sampler, drop episodes over 1 mm and down-weight the rest in the PPO update because the agent otherwise exploits the overlap; strict success rises from under 40% to 85-88%.
neighbors.difference: States the exploit clause for GPU contact-rich RL and attributes the artefact to real-time execution (cap, step and collision model bundled); never isolates the cap; no 2x2.

neighbors.title: Assessing Transferability from Simulation to Reality for Reinforcement Learning (SPOTA)
neighbors.trick: Define simulation optimisation bias as the optimiser's gain from exploiting simulator error, estimate it from held-out randomised domains and stop training when the estimate says the policy is over-fitted.
neighbors.difference: The exploit clause as a defined, estimated quantity (2019); parametric error, held-out domains as reference; the claim's interaction term is SOB with the converged engine as the held-out domain.

neighbors.title: Sim2Real Predictivity: Does Evaluation in Simulation Predict Real-World Performance?
neighbors.trick: Run nine navigation agents in a scanned lab and its replica, define the sim-vs-real correlation coefficient, find 0.18 because agents exploit collision dynamics to slide along walls, tune the simulator to 0.84.
neighbors.difference: Single-artefact exploit datum on collision handling, post hoc; no cap, no isolated knob.

neighbors.title: PolySim: Bridging the Sim-to-Real Gap for Humanoid Control via Multi-Simulator Dynamics Randomization
neighbors.trick: Train one humanoid controller across Isaac Sim, Isaac Gym and Genesis at once, bound the simulator inductive bias, and measure the exploit as the sim-to-sim success drop in MuJoCo (+52.8 points).
neighbors.difference: Whole-engine exploit measured in-window; the contact solver is named as a bias source and held as a fixed meta-parameter, never varied alone.

neighbors.title: MJX performance tuning page; MJWarp solver-iterations page
neighbors.trick: Lower iterations and ls_iterations until the simulation is just stable because DR noise dwarfs solver inaccuracy in RL; on MJWarp the solver early-exits once all worlds converge so the caps have less performance impact.
neighbors.difference: The trade clause and the field's assumption in the owners' words; not a measurement; weakens the speed half on Warp.

neighbors.title: Multi-Fidelity Policy Gradients Stabilize Data-Scarce Reinforcement Learning (MFPG-PPO)
neighbors.trick: Use cheap low-fidelity rollouts (coarser step, fewer solver iterations, simpler collision) only as a control variate for the high-fidelity gradient so the estimator stays unbiased.
neighbors.difference: Bundles the cap into a simplified simulator; no per-knob number, no exploit measurement; precedent for C-W43-16.

neighbors.title: Theoretical Foundations and Effective Algorithms for Policy-Aware Simulator Learning
neighbors.trick: Learn a simulator as a minimax game against an adversarial policy because RL optimisers inevitably exploit minor model inaccuracies; worst-case policy search is dual to RL on the critic's one-step error.
neighbors.difference: Exploit clause as a premise for learned models; no engineered engine, no knob.

neighbors.title: Imperfect World Models are Exploitable
neighbors.trick: A model is exploitable when it reverses the preference between two policies relative to the true dynamics; exploitation is unavoidable on large policy sets.
neighbors.difference: The definition of the quantity the 2x2 measures; no procedure, no engine; must be cited.

neighbors.title: Reinforcement Learning-Based Control for an Inline Skating Humanoid Robot

neighbors.title: MEMENTO: Teaching LLMs to Manage Their Own Context
neighbors.trick: Train a reasoning model to segment its chain of thought into blocks, summarize each, and physically evict the block's KV while keeping the summary's entries computed with the block visible; serve from a vLLM fork with block masking and train with RL under the same masking.
neighbors.difference: none — occupied: §6.2.1 is C-W43-24's same-text cache-kept-vs-rebuilt test (66.1% to 50.8% on AIME24, −15.3 pp); App. A.2.3 trains under physical KV compaction with a matched block-mask trainer (C-W44-10's g_op as default); untrained models, tool outputs and agent benchmarks are its own future work

neighbors.title: MemoryWalker: Stop Training Agents on Contexts They Never Saw
neighbors.trick: Treat a rollout under mid-trajectory context compression as a tree of conditioning branches, show that replaying the final context or the full history both train the wrong distributions, and recover exactness with a K-forward traversal or a packed 4D mask from eviction records (or approximately by self-distillation).
neighbors.difference: none — occupied on the trainer half: train–rollout log-prob gap 0.366 vs 0.014 floor (26x) on eviction-heavy batches; 4D mask proven gradient-equivalent (Theorem 1); text-level editors on SGLang re-prefill rather than cache-level drops, same dense-attention construction

neighbors.title: Context Language Models
neighbors.trick: Let the model edit its context as a file, train the editing with stepwise GRPO, and serve edits with Suffix Cache Reuse that keeps the unchanged suffix's KV computed under the pre-edit context and re-rotates positions.
neighbors.difference: serving-side ghost channel used on purpose at matched accuracy, approximation named (App. B) and capped at K = 6 spans; RL rollouts served without it; cites Memento for the retained-information finding

neighbors.title: Sparse-RL: Breaking the Memory Wall in LLM Reinforcement Learning via Stable Sparse Rollouts
neighbors.trick: Run RL rollouts under KV compression and correct the resulting off-policy bias with sparsity-aware rejection sampling and importance reweighting.
neighbors.difference: states the trainer half as its premise (dense old policy vs sparse sampler policy vs learner); single-turn reasoning, no agent loop, no eviction record

neighbors.title: How to Compress KV Cache in RL Post-Training? Shadow Mask Distillation for Memory-Efficient Alignment
neighbors.trick: Sampler acts under a sparse context while the learner updates under the dense one; importance reweighting fails, so distill the sparse-context behaviour.
neighbors.difference: same premise and register; names the failure of the correction family C-W44-09/10 would test; single-turn

neighbors.title: Sparrow: Sparse Rollout for Stable and Efficient Long-context RL of Large Language Models
neighbors.trick: Keep the lower tail of per-token sparse-to-dense actor-policy mismatch above a threshold by scheduling sparsity during generation.
neighbors.difference: per-token mismatch ruler used as the stability control (C-W43-25's shape); sparse attention, single-turn

neighbors.title: KV4-RL: Unlocking Faster Asynchronous Rollouts for RLVR with INT4 KV Cache Quantization
neighbors.trick: Quantize the rollout KV cache to INT4 while protecting attention sinks and recent context in INT8 because sampler mismatch concentrates there.
neighbors.difference: cache-state mismatch from quantization, not eviction; attention-sink vocabulary inside RL

neighbors.title: LEGO-RL: Harness-Native Reinforcement Learning for Coding Agents
neighbors.trick: Proxy a native coding harness's LLM calls in-process so the trainer recomputes log-probabilities from the raw stream even under harness-side compaction, keeping rollout–training probability correlation above 0.99.
neighbors.difference: a shipped stack built on the trainer half's consequence (log the stream, not the transcript); text-level compaction

neighbors.title: Request Order Matters: Cache-History Sensitivity in Selective KV-Cache Reuse for Rolling Agents
neighbors.trick: Reusing non-prefix KV with selective recomputation makes a rolling agent's answer depend on earlier requests (69.0% variation with token top-k, 26.1% with document-aligned recompute).
neighbors.difference: serving-half mechanism measured as answer variation across requests rather than within one trajectory's drops

neighbors.title: InterQ-RL: Interaction-Aware Correction of Execution Mismatch in Quantized Agentic RL
neighbors.trick: Match the trainer's quantizer to the engine's, then weight each action token by the clipped prefix product of engine-versus-trainer log-ratios over earlier actions.
neighbors.difference: owns the history-level correction for the arithmetic term; assumes shared token history; no eviction

neighbors.title: On the Origin and Evolution of Training-Inference Mismatch in LLM Reinforcement Learning
neighbors.trick: Evaluate the trainer at the sampler's weights to split each token error into a constant numerical discrepancy (removed by per-prefix centering) and a policy lag that feeds back through updates.
neighbors.difference: characterizes C-W44-09's arithmetic arm (constant bias) with no eviction arm and no growth law

neighbors.title: Cache Engineering for Agents (AKV)
neighbors.trick: Drop old tool responses' KV and re-rotate survivors instead of summarizing and re-prefilling.
neighbors.difference: the card; asserts the ghost channel without a test and names training under the scheme as future work

neighbors.title: Leyline: KV Cache Directives for Agentic Inference
neighbors.trick: A serving directive lets a harness splice a span out of the cache in place or trim and re-prefill, with a closed-form RoPE correction.
neighbors.difference: ships both arms of C-W43-24 as modes and does not compare their accuracy

neighbors.title: Compression Does Not End at Selection: Post-Selection Positional Geometry for Sparse KV Caches (RoPERelay)
neighbors.trick: After selection, reassign compact RoPE coordinates by inverse rotation and re-rotation so eviction gaps do not distort matching.
neighbors.difference: the repos half of AKV on a fixed cache; no RL, no text arm

neighbors.title: ECHO: Prune To Act, Trace To Learn With Selective Turn Memory In Agentic RL
neighbors.trick: Compress each turn into a source-indexed record, rebuild bounded contexts from selected records, and route credit through the selected indices.
neighbors.difference: the consequence side of the trainer half as a recipe (with Mosaic 2610.22174 and RTPO 2608.18682); text-level

neighbors.title: Random Attention: Rethinking KV Cache Eviction for Efficient Reasoning
neighbors.trick: Evict uniformly at random per head and match scored eviction, because the trace restates what it needs and every head keeps a copy.
neighbors.difference: explains eviction survivability via redundancy; does not separate cache state from text

pre_window_precedents.trick: ReSum (2025-09): train each summarization segment under its own input and broadcast the trajectory advantage across segments.
MEM1 (2025-06): RL with a constant-size internal state that overwrites context each turn — compaction inside the policy.
Complexity Trap (2025-08): omitting older observations as text matches LLM summarization on SWE-bench Verified — the TEXT arm's accuracy claim.
CacheBlend (2024-05): reuse KV computed in another context and selectively recompute a few tokens to repair the missing cross-attention — the state is not the text.
EPIC (2024-10): position-independent KV reuse with an attention-sink fix at every document start.
Prompt Cache (2023-11): modular attention-state reuse across prompts with a schema for positional accuracy.
H2O (2023-06): keep heavy-hitter and recent entries; the retained entries carry what they aggregated.
StreamingLLM (2023-09): attention sinks let window attention run indefinitely.
Gist tokens (2023-04): entries trained on purpose to carry evicted prompt text.

limitation_quotes.quote: Future work includes extending the framework to broader compression policies (e.g., dropping tool observations or using latent summaries), testing across a broader range of harnesses, and adapting exact tree-consistent replay to sparse and linear-attention architectures.

Looking forward, we see two natural extensions: scaling the RL recipe to larger models, and applying Memento to long-horizon agent tasks where agent steps form natural blocks and context windows are the primary bottleneck.
Because the reused states were computed under the pre-edit context, Suffix Cache Reuse approximates re-prefilling

kill_search.why_not_done: The exact fix is cheaper than the measurement: with eviction records, one forward under a 4D or block mask reproduces the served conditioning for every token (MemoryWalker Theorem 1; Memento's vLLM fork and trainer, App. A.2.3), so no stack with records needs the size of the bias it removes; black-box stacks are MemoryWalker's SDCC case. Enabling pieces landed in order: ReSum 2025-09, Sparse-RL 2026-01, Memento 2026-04, MemoryWalker 2026-09, AKV 2026-10. The pressure #11 numerics evidence (vLLM post 2026-10-14: KL 2e-3 to 29.9; MoE routing flips) belongs to the arithmetic/routing line (CIS, DLC, R3/PR2/RDC) and the proposed CL-W44-04, not to this claim.

pre_window_precedents.trick: Miller 2024: treat an evaluation as an experiment drawn from a super-population; clustered standard errors, paired differences, power planning.
Agarwal et al. 2021: with few runs per task, report interval estimates and performance profiles, not point estimates.
Henderson et al. 2017: seeds and environment non-determinism make reported deep-RL improvements uninterpretable without significance metrics.
Colas et al. 2018: the number of random seeds from t-test and bootstrap power formulas.
tau-bench 2024: pass^k as the consistency metric over k runs.
HAL 2025-10-13 (19 days pre-window): 'higher reasoning effort reducing accuracy in the majority of runs' from 'single runs without statistical validation for most evaluations' — the claim's premise.

limitation_quotes.quote: One task. Everything here comes from one tabular prediction task with one dataset. The phenomena are likely to appear elsewhere; their sizes may not. Benchmarks with many tasks and pass/fail outcomes estimate how results generalise across tasks; ours estimates variation within one configuration and small effects on one task. Neither replaces the other.
Our analysis covers over 18,000 agent trajectories, but is limited to four tasks across two scientific domains. More tasks and domains would strengthen the generality of the conclusions.
Our study uses a single model, which is a core limitation.
